title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Blind Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: Can quantum advantages in computational efficiency coexist with quantum advantages in privacy? In this paper, we construct and use MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler, to answer this question with a resounding yes. We approach this question by bridging two seemingly disparate paradigms: universal blind quantum computation (UBQC), based on measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms such as the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm and quantum recommendation systems. We provide new upper bounds on the depth of UBQC brickwork graphs, establishing that $D = \mathcal{O}(ωn)$, where $ω$ is the circuit width and $n$ its computational gate complexity. This is enabled by our newly developed transpiler MasonQ, which maps arbitrary quantum circuits to computational brickwork graph states. Given an optimal Qiskit circuit as input, we prove optimality (up to logarithmic corrections) of the MasonQ transpiler in terms of asymptotic scaling of the total brickwork graph width and depth after decomposition into bricks, enabling systematic cost analyses of blind implementations in near-term experiments and asymptotic regimes. Leveraging MasonQ, we derive depth bounds for several representative blind quantum machine learning (B-QML) algorithms, including the quantum Fourier transform, the HHL algorithm, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers. Lastly, we analyze concrete resource estimates for near-term demonstrations of blind quantum machine learning. We propose a minimal B-QML implementation requiring only a $12$ qubit quantum server. To the best of our knowledge, MasonQ is the first functional and optimal universal circuit-to-brickwork-graph transpiler to implement the full brickwork transpilation process from first principles.

title: Learning to Design Convex Relaxations for Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by replacing hard nonconvex problems with convex surrogates that give valid bounds. Yet their design is still largely manual: a human expert must decide where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth is worth paying. We show that this design process can be learned. The method proposed in this paper, AutoConvexRelax, represents the symbolic formulation of a nonconvex problem as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions. It then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem-specific relaxation trajectories as the formulation evolves. We prove that finite action sequences generated by the learned policy preserve relaxation validity under explicit domain, occurrence-context, and representation-consistency conditions. We further establish computable error bounds for mixed relaxations and sufficient conditions for feasible recovery and global-optimality certification. As a first instantiation, we apply the method to nonconvex quadratic problems and fractional problems. On 241 benchmark quadratic instances, the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%. Its mean lower bound is 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations on the normalized comparison metric, while it uses substantially smaller formulations. The learned policy retains this trade-off on fractional instances and reaches near-semidefinite bounds on beamforming and sensor-network localization instances. These results suggest that convex relaxation design can move from a fixed handcrafted choice to an automated learning process that adapts to problem structures. Code is available at https://github.com/auto4opt/AutoConvexRelax.

title: EvoSpatial: Experience-Driven Skill and Tool Evolution for Spatial Reasoning Agents
abstract: Spatial reasoning agents can inspect tool outputs and repair errors, but reusing these lessons requires preserving both the computation and the conditions that make it valid. We introduce EvoSpatial, a framework that learns from execution experience by updating a library of linked skills and tools. Skills describe procedures, geometric assumptions, and verification steps; tools implement the operations those procedures require. When solving a task, the agent retrieves relevant skills and synthesizes reusable computational functions if existing tools are insufficient. After each task, execution feedback and evidence checks guide skill revision and tool consolidation, without ground-truth answers or benchmark scores. Across 20 benchmarks, EvoSpatial averages 63.9, 4.0 percentage points above the average reported by SpatialClaw. The evolved library also improves held-out and cross-benchmark performance when updates are disabled, and trajectories generated with evolved skills improve supervised fine-tuning, even without external skills at evaluation. Keeping checked procedures on record, together with the tools that support them, lets an agent carry spatial reasoning experience from one task to the next.

After each task, execution feedback and evidence checks guide skill revision and tool consolidation, without ground-truth answers or benchmark scores. Across 20 benchmarks, EvoSpatial averages 63.9, 4.0 percentage points above the average reported by SpatialClaw. The evolved library also improves held-out and cross-benchmark performance when updates are disabled, and trajectories generated with evolved skills improve supervised fine-tuning, even without external skills at evaluation. Keeping checked procedures on record, together with the tools that support them, lets an agent carry spatial reasoning experience from one task to the next.

title: Efficient agentic AI: A framework for adaptive test-time scaling, resource-aware evaluation and adaptive reasoning
abstract: Agentic AI systems leverage large reasoning models that are increasingly using longer chains of thought, parallel sampling, search, or verifier-guided refinement at test time to make use of additional compute. This additional compute is typically wasted: agents "overthink" simple sub-tasks, redo tool calls for no particular reason, and allow context to accumulate over time through long tasks. In this paper, we will study efficiency in agentic reasoning systems from six perspectives. First, a taxonomy of test-time scaling strategies for agentic workloads. Second, a multi-dimensional efficiency framework including compute, latency, tokens, cost, energy, memory and task success. Third, a conceptual description of the reasoning efficiency frontier, based on patterns of results reported in the reasoning-model literature, showing where more reasoning might be beneficial, where it ceases to be beneficial, and where it might be counterproductive. Fourth, a benchmarking approach that is not only proposed for single-turn inference but also for agentic workloads. Fifth, an Adaptive Test-time Scaling Controller with task difficulty and model uncertainty-constrained reasoning budgets. Sixth, a taxonomy of modes of failure of agentic pipelines, with examples. It is this paper's position that adaptive budgeting should realize a significant portion of the accuracy that is obtainable with maximal test-time scaling that could be obtained at a much higher compute expense. It's a conceptual finding, backed up in the frontier analysis performed in Section 5, and not a measured result. The paper additionally proposes that much of the wasted compute in agentic systems is likely to be attributable to more factors than just reasoning, such as retries, context growth and multi-agent coordination.

title: Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core: Universal Thermodynamic Homeostasis & Epistemic Multi-Anchoring
abstract: Conventional AI guardrail frameworks rely on extrinsic, post-generation text filters, regex wrappers, or trailing output classifiers. By evaluating generated text after latent state transitions have completed, extrinsic systems operate with severe diagnostic latency, introducing metastable strain and creating critical vulnerabilities to prompt injections, deceptive alignment, and reward hacking. This paper specifies the Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core—a substrate-agnostic, dual-head thermodynamic control framework for autoregressive language models. By evaluating residual stream activation kinematics in memory during prefill and decoding, the Sentinel Core constructs an invariant State Uncertainty Coordinate grounded in statistical mechanics and Landauer's Principle. The architecture partitions latent acceleration into tangential semantic velocity and orthogonal boundary shear , preserving model agentic agency via prefill-extracted context centroids while enforcing deterministic 0-token prefill eviction and 1–3 token decode vetoes Fused Top-K logit steering and a dual-tier containment architecture (userspace stream cancellation and kernel-level eBPF socket drops).

title: Context Parallax: Changing the view without losing the question
abstract: Context Parallax (CPX) studies a declared change of conversational frame while keeping the question, permitted evidence and authority record explicit. This first public edition presents a comparison contract, a bounded model pilot, finite constructions and a scoped Lean companion. The recognition pilot comprises 432 calls on twelve previously inspected fictional cases, three carries, two instruction phrasings and three Qwen configurations. Plain and recipient-frame guidance selected the same answer in every matched pair. Local 4B and 9B scored 140/144 and 144/144 on the frozen answer-and-format endpoint. Hosted 32B scored 0/144 under the strict JSON parser; a separately labeled post-hoc removal of enclosing Markdown fences yielded 140/144. The result establishes no framing advantage, population effect or causal model-size effect. The formal companion checks 33 selected declarations in four claim families: attained-capsule decoding, protected return, finite rational optional information, and question-relative resolution with an intervention counterexample. Five modules passed replay by Lean's own kernel. Cached imports remain trusted, and the source-to-formal review is a self-review. The full manuscript, model pilot, broader language-benefit hypothesis and claims about experience are outside this formal coverage. The companion ZIP provides editable manuscript sources, frozen requests and retained responses, strict and supplementary scoring, finite-study code and evidence, review dispositions, exact proof sources, dependency pins, historical failures and source crosswalks. It includes an offline Python verification route and separate instructions for the formal replay. No model calls are needed to inspect or replay the retained computations. Private full conversations, raw reviewer conversations, model weights and third-party reading PDFs are excluded. Christopher Daniel Pang is the human author and steward. Hearthline is the named AI collaborator, contributing conceptual synthesis, research, drafting and implementation. The paper preserves the separate naming and correction history of Context Parallax, pinch, inflection and seed. Six model reviews and a companion addendum informed the earlier revision; no independent human peer review is claimed. Version 1.0 is a completed research preprint. Original release material is shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), with existing third-party rights preserved. Broader empirical questions remain open.

title: Walking Through the Catalog: Designing Immersive Access to CIDOC-CRM Cultural-Heritage Collections
abstract: Galleries, libraries, archives, and museums increasingly publish their catalogs as linked open data structured by CIDOC-CRM, an event-centric ontology in which people, objects, places, and documents are connected through the events of their shared histories. Making these event chains inspectable alongside collection records is an access-design challenge. We investigate immersive access as an alternative: an XR client that renders a CIDOC-CRM collection as an explorable spatial graph, retrieved on demand from a live, configured SPARQL endpoint. We contribute (1) six design requirements for immersive access to event-centric heritage linked data, grounded in the digital-library literature; (2) an ontology-driven mapping from CIDOC-CRM constructs to a spatial-graph representation, partially implemented in a working prototype; and (3) an author-conducted analytical evaluation that combines a requirements walkthrough with a quantitative characterization of a live heritage endpoint, identifying where the design holds and where collection-scale realities strain it. No user study was conducted.

title: Automated whole slide Allred score estimation for estrogen receptor assessment in breast cancer
abstract: Accurate assessment of estrogen receptor (ER) status is critical in breast cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, as it directly determines eligibility for endocrine therapy. ER expression is routinely evaluated on immunohistochemistry (IHC) slides using the semi-quantitative Allred scoring system, which combines the proportion of ER-positive tumor nuclei with staining intensity into a composite score of 0–8. However, manual Allred scoring is labor-intensive, subjective, and prone to inter- and intra-observer variability, particularly in cases that are borderline. In this work, we present a whole-slide image (WSI)-level Allred score estimation pipeline built around MOSAIC, our previously developed multi-scale, orientation-aware nuclei analysis network. The pipeline incorporates a patch-based WSI inference strategy that requires only nucleus-level annotations for training; a centroid-guided instance separation and majority-voting scheme that converts pixel-level segmentation outputs into clinically interpretable proportion scores and intensity scores; and a systematic aggregation protocol that derives the final Allred score without requiring slide-level supervision. MOSAIC integrates multi-scale context extraction to handle nuclear size variability, rotation-enhanced fusion to improve robustness to arbitrary nuclear orientation, and a transformer-inspired multi-scale integration hub to model long-range contextual dependencies across heterogeneous tissue regions. Experimental evaluation on an institutional ER-IHC cohort comprising 37 WSIs from different patients demonstrated strong pixel-level segmentation accuracy, robust instance-level nuclei detection, and improved stability in borderline ER cases. At the WSI level, the pipeline achieved the highest concordance with pathologist-assigned hormonal therapy decisions (89.2%) among all compared approaches, requiring an average of 3.5 minutes to analyze the pathologist-defined tumor regions of each WSI, compared with 11 minutes to 2 hours for the baseline methods evaluated under the present experimental protocol.

title: Efficient Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment for Latent Generative Models
abstract: Fréchet Distributional (FD) objectives provide an effective distribution-level signal for post-training generative models. For latent generative models, however, existing FD-based post-training methods optimize only the latent generator while keeping the decoder frozen: the decoder is trained on reconstruction latents obtained from real images but deployed on generator-produced latents at generation time. When these latent distributions differ, this \textbf{decoder train-generation mismatch} means that the decoder is deployed on inputs drawn from a distribution it was not directly trained on. We introduce \textbf{Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA)}, an efficient post-training method that freezes the latent generator and directly optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents using an FD objective. A single epoch of FDDA consistently improves gFID and gFDr$^6$ across diverse flow-based and autoregressive latent generative models. Across all 11 evaluated models, FDDA reduces gFDr$^6$ by 34.0-59.6\% from the original pretrained models and provides a further 10.2-57.2\% reduction after generator-side FD post-training. FDDA also reduces total wall-clock time by factors of $3.6\times$-$328.7\times$ relative to generator-side FD post-training across these models. These results show that generator-side post-training alone does not exhaust the benefits of FD optimization, and that further gains can be obtained by adapting the decoder at substantially lower cost.

title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

title: Machine Learning Models Trained on a Longitudinal Survey Dataset Poorly Predict Hundreds of Life Outcomes
abstract: Understanding the predictability of life outcomes is important for public policy and science, but existing studies focus on a limited number of outcomes and therefore struggle to describe the broad patterns of predictability. We developed a high-throughput approach that uses a single dataset to study the predictability of many future outcomes using past data. We deployed this approach with hundreds of outcomes and thousands of machine learning models per outcome in the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study. Three findings emerged. First, most outcomes were not very predictable, but some were much more predictable than others. Second, even for the most predictable outcomes, our complex prediction procedure typically exhibited little skill relative to a simple procedure. Third, we found modest patterns in how predictability varied across outcomes. We conclude by discussing scope conditions and how future research might address them.

title: Amortized Variational Inference of Latent Intensities from Replicated Point Patterns
abstract: Bayesian inference for latent point process intensities often relies on per-dataset sampling or optimization, making repeated inference computationally expensive. We propose a neural-network-based amortized variational framework that learns a reusable inference rule mapping a variable number of replicated point patterns to a distribution over their shared latent intensity. Trained from event times using the point process likelihood, the model learns an amortized inference rule without ground-truth intensity supervision. At test time, it performs inference of the latent distribution in a forward pass. On synthetic data, additional realizations improve intensity recovery and yield narrower credible intervals with broadly stable coverage. Our method is tested on bicycle-sharing data and achieves the highest mean held-out log likelihood among the evaluated methods while requiring substantially less inference time than the Log-Gaussian Cox Process baseline.

title: VisExMEM: Visual Evidence-Based Explainable Multimodal Evaluation Metric
abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation. For untuned Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol controls, decomposed prompting raises the same composite by 3.6-5.1 points relative to holistic prompting. Human evaluation shows that VisExMEM explanations outperform prior explainable metrics and approach GPT-5.6 Sol.

title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.

evidence.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
evidence.abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.

title: INMAD V.2 LaBSE Alignment Audit: Scored Corpus, Analysis Notebook and Results
abstract: This record supports the article “Cross-Lingual Semantic Alignment Analysis of Indonesian–Madurese Parallel Corpus using Language-Agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding (LaBSE)” (submitted to JOIN – Jurnal Online Informatika). It provides LaBSE cosine-similarity scores for all 23,086 English–Indonesian–Madurese triples of the INMAD V.2 corpus (doi:10.17632/dt7d8dmfgs.2), the Google Colab notebook that reproduces every number, table and figure of the article, and the derived tables, figures and quality flags. Contents INMAD_V2_LaBSE_scores.csv: the corpus with Indonesian–Madurese, English–Madurese and Indonesian–English scores, word counts, quality flags, the corpus part (manual or back-translated) and links between rows that share a Madurese sentence. LaBSE_INMAD_Revision_Analysis_v3.ipynb: the analysis notebook (sentence-transformers/LaBSE, Google Colab with a T4 GPU). Tables 2–4, the NusaX control, Figures 2–4, the 2,156 triples flagged by the provisional noise-floor rule, and the 272-word Madurese stopword list used for the word clouds. Main resultsLaBSE gives a mean similarity of 0.86 for Indonesian–English but 0.52 for Indonesian–Madurese and 0.54 for English–Madurese, and ranks the correct Madurese translation first for only 40.8% of the Indonesian sentences. On NusaX, Madurese scores 0.56, while the LaBSE-supported Javanese and Sundanese score 0.89, so most of the gap reflects the encoder’s limited coverage of Madurese. INMAD rows whose Indonesian side was created by back-translation score lower than manually translated rows (0.45 versus 0.58). Note for usersRows 1–11,541 contain the manually translated sentences; rows 11,542–23,086 contain back-translated Indonesian paraphrases paired with the same Madurese translations. Keep linked rows (twin_row_id) in the same split when training or evaluating MT systems. See README.md for column definitions, methods and reproduction steps.

title: A Hybrid Dimensionality Reduction and Spectral Classification Workflow for Mineral Mapping in Polar Terrains
abstract: Accurate identification of alteration minerals in remote polar regions remains a significant challenge because field access is limited, environmental conditions are extreme, and exposed lithologies commonly show mixed spectral responses. Satellite-based multispectral remote sensing, particularly using the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER), provides an efficient means of investigating surface mineralogy in ice-free Antarctic terrains. This study applies a sequential dimensionality reduction and spectral classification workflow integrating Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Independent Component Analysis (ICA), Minimum Noise Fraction (MNF), and Mixture-Tuned Matched Filtering (MTMF) to ASTER imagery from the Dry Valleys of South Victoria Land, Antarctica. The workflow identified major mineral groups including iron oxides and hydroxides, Al–OH and Mg–OH phyllosilicates, carbonates, silica phases, and mafic–ultramafic indicator minerals. These mapped mineral groups are spatially associated with granitoid and metasedimentary basement rocks, Beacon Supergroup sedimentary units, Jurassic diabase intrusions, and Ferrar volcanic rocks. Accuracy assessment against lithological reference classes indicated an overall accuracy of about 78% and a kappa coefficient of approximately 0.72. The results show that the integrated ASTER workflow can support regional mineral group mapping in exposed polar bedrock terrains, while individual mineral interpretations remain limited by ASTER spectral resolution, mixed pixels, and restricted field validation.

title: Evidence-Centered Histopathological Grading of Prostate Cancer : A Review of Machine Learning, Hybrid CNN–Transformer Models, Fusion, and Explainable AI
abstract: Automated Gleason grading of prostate biopsy histopathology has progressed from handcrafted colour and texture descriptors with conventional classifiers to deep convolutional networks, ensembles, attention and transformer models, hybrid CNN–ViT pipelines, and federated and multi-institutional validation efforts. Recent studies report very high tile-level accuracy, but some persistent problems remain: the grade classes are unequal in size and adjacent grades are hard to separate, evaluation is dominated by accuracy, patient-level, slide-level and external testing is uncommon, and the quality of explanations is rarely measured quantitatively. In this review, we categorize grading methods into handcrafted and classical machine learning, convolutional and transfer-learning systems, ensemble and label-noise-aware models, attention, transformer and hybrid pipelines, and fusion, multimodal and federated approaches. Comparative analysis shows that reported performance is strongly shaped by dataset composition, image resolution, label definition (Gleason pattern versus ISUP grade group), preprocessing and split design, so architectural contributions cannot be ranked from headline figures alone. Evidence-centered grading is therefore not a single network but a combination of complementary local and global representations, grade-aware prediction, calibrated uncertainty, and clinically grounded explainable AI. Priority directions identified in this review include leakage-safe patient-level splitting, slide-level aggregation, multi-centre external validation, calibration reporting, quantitative assessment of explanations, and integration of histology with clinical evidence.

title: Моделирование нечетких систем управления в программной среде MATLAB
abstract: Соответствует содержанию дисциплины «Проектирование интеллектуальных систем управления» для подготовки бакалавров по направлению подготовки 27.03.04 «Управление в технических системах». В пособии изложены основы теории нечеткой логики и практические методы построения нечетких систем управления в программной среде MATLAB с использованием Fuzzy Logic Toolbox. Рассматриваются лингвистические переменные, функции принадлежности, база правил, методы нечеткого вывода Мамдани и Сугено, дефаззификация, проектирование и валидация нечетких моделей. Практическая часть включает в себя примеры и лабораторные работы по разработке регуляторов и систем принятия решений для типовых инженерных объектов. Предназначено студентов бакалавриата инженерных специальностей.

title: Structured Knowledge Graph for Scholarly Exploration: IR and QA System for ETDs and their Elements
abstract: Electronic Theses and Dissertations (ETDs) contain rich and detailed scholarly knowledge, but accessing that remains difficult. Conventional search systems largely operate at the document level and provide only coarse access to long-form academic writing. Though large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses, those often lack reliable grounding in the internal structure and semantic relationships of ETDs. We address these challenges with a knowledge graph (KG) framework for scholarly exploration and LLM-aided question answering (QA) over ETDs and their elements.

title: AI4Optics: private, locally hosted AI chatbot for optical metrology that leverages AI advantages while protecting company know-how
abstract: This project “AI4Optics” addresses the challenge of knowledge preservation and utilization in small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs) within the optical measurement industry. SMEs face the risk of losing valuable domain knowledge as experienced employees retire and industry requirements evolve. The project therefore aims to develop a domain-specific chatbot that enables efficient and secure access to internal company knowledge. The system is based on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, combining semantic search with generative language models. User queries are matched with relevant content from a locally hosted knowledge base, and the retrieved information is used to generate context-aware responses. Company documents—such as ERP data, technical manuals, and engineering records—are processed in a structured pipeline: segmented into smaller text units, converted into semantic vectors using embedding models, and stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval. This enables the chatbot to identify relevant information even when queries differ linguistically from the original sources. A key aspect of the approach is the use of a fully local data infrastructure. The chatbot can be deployed on-premise, ensuring that sensitive company knowledge remains on internal servers and is not transmitted to external cloud services. In addition to internal documentation, this concept can be extended to external but controlled datasets, such as conference proceedings—for example, those from IMEKO. Instead of publishing such content openly on the internet, it can be stored on a secure local server and made accessible through a dedicated chatbot interface. This would allow engineers and researchers to query the complete body of conference knowledge efficiently while maintaining full control over data access. Similarly, this system can be fully customised for a specific company and utilise its own company-specific database. It is therefore a completely independent system and can be adapted for any type of business. This approach addresses a growing concern: currently, many conference proceedings are published freely online, making them accessible not only to the research community but also to external AI systems. As a result, proprietary knowledge, innovative ideas, and engineering solutions may be unintentionally used to train third-party models, potentially leading to a loss of competitive advantage. By contrast, a locally hosted chatbot ensures that knowledge remains protected within a defined environment—accessible to authorized users, but not distributed publicly or absorbed into external AI ecosystems. Initial evaluations show that such chatbot systems can effectively support engineering-related tasks, including material selection, design decisions, and troubleshooting. They provide features such as natural language interaction, transparent source referencing, multilingual capabilities, and real-time response generation. Overall, the project demonstrates the strong potential of domain-specific, locally deployed AI systems to preserve critical knowledge, enhance process efficiency, and protect intellectual property, while enabling controlled and efficient access to valuable technical information.

title: An FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Network for Spatiotemporal Pattern Learning and Classification
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but efficient deployment and on-device adaptation require specialized hardware. In this work, we present an FPGA implementation of multilayer SNNs for spatiotemporal pattern classification, in which both inference and training take place on the same hardware. Our design adopts a temporal-forward-only training algorithm that avoids the memory and latency overhead associated with traditional Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). A mixed-precision scheme balances training stability with resource efficiency, and architectural optimization maximizes hardware and memory utilization. We further identify and resolve hazards that arise when inference and learning share the same memory, including port conflicts between the forward and backward access patterns and read-after-write dependencies in floating-point potential accumulation. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and five multivariate time-series classification datasets demonstrate that, with fully on-chip training, our SNN model achieves accuracy comparable to SNN or LSTM trained with BPTT. Compared to CPU and GPU based implementations, our FPGA design delivers 2.5 to 6 times higher throughput while consuming an order of magnitude less energy per sample.

title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.

title: Realistic simulation of universal multiport interferometers with losses within a Gaussian formalism
abstract: Photonic technologies are among the leading platform contenders for demonstrating quantum advantage. Nevertheless, photon losses represent the major hurdle for the realization of a fault-tolerant optical quantum computer, and the need for an accurate characterization of this phenomenon is crucial for classical simulations of quantum algorithms on noisy backends. The noisy regime would require the simulation of the algorithm on a Fock backend or rather assuming the a priori hypothesis on the uniformity of the optical losses, which may lead to wrong predictions about the outcome from the algorithm on a cerain hardware. We propose a Gaussian model that can reproduce a lossy dynamics through the experimental characterization of imperfect interferometers, yielding the corresponding mean vector and the covariance matrix. Such model can be adapted to any continuous-variable architecture (spatial or time-bin encoded) and for both the Gaussian boson sampling or general-dyne based algorithms. Eventually, we quantify the drift of optical losses from being uniform throughout the multiport interferometer by a numerical simulation. This work proposes a blueprint for future characterizations, tailor-suited for specific devices and architectures, as well as for potential error correction and mitigation techniques, and it paves the way for realistic simulations of quantum algorithms on NISQ optical platforms.

title: Revisiting Natural Language Prompts from Large Language Models for Open-Vocabulary Video Recognition
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP have shown great success in image tasks, however, applying CLIP to open-vocabulary video recognition poses challenges. Due to the limited text information, directly fine-tuning CLIP on video recognition datasets may lead to overfitting and hinder its generalizability. A prevalent method is to enrich text information by generating prompts using Large Language Models (LLMs). However, limited efforts have been made to explore how to generate higher-quality prompts that can contribute to classify unseen categories, and how to further enhance vision-text alignment based on these prompts. In this paper, we propose P2CLIP (Prompt-guided CLIP), which aims to bridge this gap by exploring the impact of prompts across three aspects: category, video, and frame. At the category level, we argue that LLM-generated prompts under simple instructions may suffer from semantic overgeneralization, which can blur the category boundaries and hinder the performance of the model. To address this issue, we design Generic-Discriminative Prompt using LLMs to obtain discriminative category embeddings with rich semantic information. At the video and frame levels, we first use VLM and LLM to generate frame and video descriptions for enhancing vision-text alignment. title: The Personal Agent, Built by Hand: A Statement of Prior Work
abstract: On October 12, 2026, Meta announced Muse Wonder, headlining 'Active Memory' and 'Active Focus.' title: Does the Evidence a Model Cites Drive Its Conclusion? A Pre-registered Causal Test of Declared Evidence Relations in Structured Reasoning Traces
abstract: When a language model writes down its reasoning, does the evidence it cites actually drive the conclusion it states? We contribute a reproducible method for testing causal alignment between declared trace relations and model computation, and a pre-registered application to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a controlled comparison task. Models emit typed, machine-checkable reasoning traces in Scholialang, where a Finding atom declares its dependence on an Evidence atom. We test that declared edge by activation patching: we splice a counterfactual Evidence span's activations into the clean context and check whether the Finding's read is redirected as the relation predicts. For this model and task, a model's emitted symbolic label can causally steer its subsequent conclusion, even when the accompanying facts disagree. On the same 90 self-generated chains, patching the cited span redirected the conclusion in 77/90 relations when the twin flipped both numbers and label. Flipping only the polarity label (supports/refutes) redirected it in 73/90 (paired with the full twin: 84.4% agreement, McNemar p = 0.424). Swapping only the numbers never changed the selected status under this intervention (0/90), although in a post-hoc analysis it shifted the decision margin toward the counterfactual status in every case, by about 27% as much as the label flip. A donor that changed only the Evidence text redirected exactly the same 77 relations as the full twin. What we establish is downstream label influence. Where the numeric comparison is computed, and whether the declared reference structure itself controls routing, remain open: we did not intervene on how the label was generated. The supporting results were pre-registered. Validation, where task relevance is known by construction, separates relevant from irrelevant evidence (J = 1.000 in both evidence orders; per-class Wilson lower bound ≈ 0.862). Redirection rates on two batteries were 77/90 and 53/71 (roughly 75–86%, with substantial between-battery variance). Redirection also succeeds when the relevant evidence is second, although broader position effects are not ruled out. Every redirection failure showed a joint evidence-plus-observation response, and unrelated-evidence controls never redirected. Behavioral arms on two hosted models show direction-sensitivity to their own evidence edits, but an authority-cue arm induced no unfaithfulness, so we have not shown that the method detects genuine unfaithfulness.

title: Fair-VARO SUMO Simulation Data and Experimental Results
abstract: This dataset accompanies the manuscript “Fair-VARO: Balancing Reliability and Participation Fairness in Vehicular Federated Learning.” The study investigates the trade-off between update completion reliability and successful-participation fairness in vehicular federated learning using SUMO-based traffic simulations and a GRU traffic-state classifier. Fair-VARO combines vehicle-state reliability scoring with compensation based on successful aggregation histories. The experimental evaluation covers different data heterogeneity levels, component ablations, controlled state–data permutations, explicit wireless completion models, an independent simulated road network, parameter sensitivity, and controlled state-report falsification. Update failures, successful-participation fairness, aggregation-weighted label representation, and predictive performance are evaluated separately. The data are generated through simulation and do not represent measurements collected from an operational vehicle fleet. Third-party data and licensing: The primary road-network materials include OpenStreetMap data (© OpenStreetMap contributors). The source file SUMO/primary/map.osm and applicable OpenStreetMap-derived road-network data remain subject to the Open Database License (ODbL); see https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright. The selected CC BY 4.0 license applies only to materials for which the authors hold the relevant rights and does not replace third-party licenses.

title: Efficient Multilingual Dependency Parsing with LoRA- Tuned LLaMA Models on CPU: A Comparative Study in Resource-Constrained Environments
abstract: Large language models&s; ability to process multilingual dependencies without the need for powerful graphics cards is being investigated more and more in current research. The goal of this research is to improve these systems&s; efficiency so they can operate entirely on traditional CPUs. The study assesses models of 1B, 3B, and 7B LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 parameters using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) as an efficient fine-tuning method. Italian, English, French, and Spanish data sets from the Universal Dependencies Database were used for the tests. LORA can rapidly train and infer while maintaining cheap hardware and power costs, according to trials carried out on the Apple Silicon and Google Cloud CPU platforms. The CPU-only LORA solution is a practical and affordable alternative for multilingual parsing, even if GPU-dependent systems like BERT and GPT-3 achieve marginally better performance. The latter method is particularly helpful for institutions and researchers without dedicated GPU resources.

title: Calibration-assisted stress-optic phase programming for a 3D-printed optical neural-network frontend
abstract: We report a calibration-assisted stress-optic phase-programming method for a 3D-printed optical neural-network (ONN) frontend. Full-vector stress-optic modeling gives a full-stress effective-index shift of Δ ⁢ 𝑛 e f f = − 2 . 1 2 8 4 × 1 0 − 4 at 850 nm, setting the phase-length rule for Mach–Zehnder interferometer (MZI) phase shifters. A matched MPB modal proxy reproduces the modeled phase sensitivity with a ratio of 0.999,396, giving phase errors below 0 . 0 0 1 2 ⁢ 𝜋 for the evaluated 4- and 8-node phase sets. MZI measurements across three annealing conditions show a monotonic reduction in fringe-shift magnitude; a separately defined ± 5 % gain-error envelope is used only for sensitivity analysis. The shortest 𝑠 = 1 design is tolerance-limited, but an 𝑠 d e s i g n = 0 . 8 5 process window restores a simulated 100% pass rate under ideal one-time per-node gain estimates, with a 17.65% length penalty. Mapping the resulting phase noise into a 64-mode MNIST optical-front-end benchmark gives 83.44% ideal accuracy and calibrated recovery of the ideal numerical reference. Mode-field maps and a stage-resolved projected | 𝐸 | 2 propagation map visualize the physical basis and propagation path while preserving the distinction between transverse modal fields and system-level power interpolation.

title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.

title: CultureBot: A Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Exploration of Cultural Heritage Data
abstract: Digital cultural heritage collections encode rich relations among objects, places, periods, providers, images, and source institutions, yet users typically access them through keyword search and faceted browsing. We present CULTUREBOT, an interactive framework for natural-language exploration of cultural heritage collections that combines knowledge-graph-guided retrieval, lexical-semantic retrieval, and source-linked generation. CULTUREBOT maps user queries to structured catalogue relations, enriches retrieved records with textual evidence, and generates answers that link back to the underlying repository records. We instantiate the framework on 81,852 SearchCulture records and release an online demonstration. In an expert evaluation involving six cultural-heritage specialists, 55 persona-grounded queries, and 250 evaluations, the graph-guided system was rated significantly higher than two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation, with the largest gains in evidence grounding, diversity, reasoning, and completeness. These results support graph-guided retrieval as a practical way to expose the relational structure of cultural collections through conversational access while preserving links to catalogue evidence.

title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation
abstract: Silicon microring resonators are promising components for photonic reservoir computing because their nonlinear optical response can transform signals and retain information about recent inputs. Under constant optical excitation, their coupled free-carrier and thermal dynamics can generate self-pulsing: a periodic output response. However, constant-input behavior does not reveal how these dynamics respond to randomly modulated signals or whether their memory is useful for temporal processing. Here, we characterize a single silicon microring resonator and a passive network of microring resonators under random input modulation. The temporal component associated with self-pulsing remains observable under random modulation, but the largest fading memory occurs near the self-pulsing boundary, where no resolved self-pulsing-like oscillation is present. reservoir computing metrics, such as memory capacity, map this accessible memory, and its decay provides effective timescales associated mainly with free-carrier and thermal relaxation. Finally, we use NARMA reconstruction to test whether the measured memory profile supports nonlinear temporal processing. Responses with a resolved self-pulsing-like component perform worse on this task, and the intrinsic memory profile is not matched to the required input history. These results show that reservoir computing metrics can characterize nonlinear microring resonator dynamics even when the physical system is not an effective standalone reservoir for the selected task.

title: Pathfinder-BP: A Low-Latency Recursive Decoder for Topological Codes
abstract: We propose Pathfinder-BP, a recursive decoder for topological quantum codes that combines belief propagation with controlled bit-flipping. An initial BP pass identifies and permanently fixes high-confidence errors. Upon convergence failure, the decoder recursively explores alternative error patterns by tentatively flipping low-confidence variables. On surface codes, Pathfinder-BP achieves a noise threshold and logical error rate comparable to minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM). A crucial advantage of Pathfinder-BP is its highly parallelizable structure, which yields a worst-case decoding latency quasi-linear in the code distance, making it a suitable candidate for low-latency hardware implementation.

title: Reducing Context and Generation Traffic in a Local-First LLM Orchestrator: A Transferability Case Study
abstract: This technical note reports a bounded transferability experiment in the Local Frontier Orchestrator (LFO), a local-first conversational architecture combining a small local language model with selective escalation to a stronger remote model. The optimization direction was materially informed by Daniel Correa Villa's Pushing Four Raspberry Pis to the Memory Wall. Rather than reproducing the Raspberry Pi experiment, this work evaluates whether its broader architecture-first principle — eliminating unnecessary computation and data/context movement before relying on hardware-specific tuning — transfers to a substantially different environment. Two selectively activated LFO optimizations were evaluated: a compact read schema that removes unused model output fields on protected read-only turns, and a lean read policy that removes write-extraction instructions from the corresponding input context. In a four-observation correctness-gated pilot, input decreased from 1756 to 1210 tokens and mean output from 173 to 24 tokens. All four answers were correct and persistent L1/L2 memory remained unchanged. Mean observed complete-turn time decreased from 159.629 s to 24.791 s, although unequal cache and model-load conditions prevent interpreting the exact latency difference as a general or statistically established speedup. The principal result is therefore architectural rather than numerical: eliminating model-visible work that is known in advance to be unnecessary substantially reduced prompt and generation traffic while preserving behavior within the tested boundary. The report also documents negative and deferred variants, including an aggressively shortened extraction policy, grouped extraction output, and an alternative placement of retrieved evidence. Source code, frozen implementation state, experimental records, and reproducibility materials are available in the public Local Frontier Orchestrator repository.

Rather than reproducing the Raspberry Pi experiment, this work evaluates whether its broader architecture-first principle — eliminating unnecessary computation and data/context movement before relying on hardware-specific tuning — transfers to a substantially different environment. Two selectively activated LFO optimizations were evaluated: a compact read schema that removes unused model output fields on protected read-only turns, and a lean read policy that removes write-extraction instructions from the corresponding input context. In a four-observation correctness-gated pilot, input decreased from 1756 to 1210 tokens and mean output from 173 to 24 tokens. All four answers were correct and persistent L1/L2 memory remained unchanged. Mean observed complete-turn time decreased from 159.629 s to 24.791 s, although unequal cache and model-load conditions prevent interpreting the exact latency difference as a general or statistically established speedup. The principal result is therefore architectural rather than numerical: eliminating model-visible work that is known in advance to be unnecessary substantially reduced prompt and generation traffic while preserving behavior within the tested boundary. The report also documents negative and deferred variants, including an aggressively shortened extraction policy, grouped extraction output, and an alternative placement of retrieved evidence. Source code, frozen implementation state, experimental records, and reproducibility materials are available in the public Local Frontier Orchestrator repository.

title: Indian Private Hospital Lung Cancer Histopathology Image Dataset (IPH-LCHID)
abstract: Official Dataset Name: Indian Private Hospital Lung Cancer Histopathology Image Dataset (IPH-LCHID) Short Name: IPH Lung Cancer Image Set Version: 1.0 Release Type: Research and educational use under institutional terms Funding Organization / Company: Xstoxservices Technologies Private Limited Geographic Origin of Specimens: Private hospital network, India Imaging Modality: Digital histopathology (hematoxylin and eosin stained tissue patches) Total Images: 15,000 Number of Classes: 3 Lung benign tissue — 5,000 images Lung adenocarcinoma — 5,000 images Lung squamous cell carcinoma — 5,000 images Images per Class: 5,000 1. Overview and Purpose The Indian Private Hospital Lung Cancer Histopathology Image Dataset (IPH-LCHID) is a curated collection of lung tissue microscopy images assembled to support machine learning, computer vision, medical imaging research, and educational study of lung cancer related histopathological patterns. The dataset contains fifteen thousand JPEG images evenly distributed across three clinically meaningful categories: lung benign tissue, lung adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma. Each class contributes exactly five thousand samples, providing a balanced foundation for supervised classification, transfer learning, weakly supervised analysis, and comparative benchmarking of deep learning architectures on lung cancer related visual patterns. Lung cancer remains one of the most consequential oncological challenges worldwide, and India carries a substantial clinical burden associated with delayed diagnosis, heterogeneous presentation, and limited access to specialist pathology review in many regions. High quality annotated image resources that reflect real hospital workflows can accelerate the development of decision support tools, triage systems, and teaching materials. IPH-LCHID was prepared with that motivation: to offer a clean, class balanced, and well documented lung cancer image corpus grounded in private hospital pathology practice in India, while remaining practical for academic laboratories, student projects, and industrial research teams exploring computational pathology. The dataset preparation, curation, quality control, documentation, and release packaging were funded and stewarded by Xstoxservices Technologies Private Limited. The company supported the digital organization of histopathology samples, class folder restructuring, metadata documentation, and preparation of this public facing description so that researchers can understand provenance, intended use, and constraints. Xstoxservices Technologies Private Limited is identified as both the funder and the company responsible for dataset packaging for this release. Any acknowledgements in academic papers, technical reports, theses, posters, software repositories, or commercial research notes that use IPH-LCHID should explicitly name Xstoxservices Technologies Private Limited as the funding and stewardship organization for the dataset release.

title: Wie wir KI verstehen und erleben
abstract: Zusammenfassung Es wird untersucht, wie generative Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) bei der Nutzung konzeptualisiert und kommunikativ erlebt wird. Im Mittelpunkt stehen mentale Modelle, Erwartungen sowie die Zuschreibung sozialer Eigenschaften und Kompetenzen an KI-Systeme. Dabei wird eruiert, ob und in welchem Ausmaß KI als greifbar, nützlich oder bedrohlich wahrgenommen wird. Angesichts der zunehmenden Verbreitung generativer KI in professionellen und alltäglichen Kontexten – etwa in der Gesundheitskommunikation, dem Online-Marketing oder der Teamarbeit – stellt sich weitergehend die Frage nach dem Erfolg des Einsatzes von KI. Erste empirische Befunde weisen darauf hin, dass diese sehr erfolgreich mit den Nutzenden kommuniziert. Der Beitrag diskutiert, welche Faktoren dieses kommunikative Gelingen begünstigen und welche Implikationen sich daraus für den zukünftigen Umgang mit KI ergeben.

title: A Limit of AI, I: A Discrete Information-Theoretic Proof of the Certainty–Scope Conjecture
abstract: Abstract Floridi’s Certainty–Scope Conjecture holds that no artificial intelligence system can be simultaneously reliable on every input and broad enough to cover the full richness of unstructured data: reliability and breadth are in structural tension, imposed by the finite information-processing capacity of any mechanism implementing intelligence. The Conjecture has until now been a philosophical thesis without a proof. This article supplies one in the finite-classification regime—the simplest non-trivial setting in which the Conjecture admits an exact statement, a sharp converse, and a matching achievability result—and is the discrete half of a coordinated diptych whose continuous companion proves a matching rate–distortion converse for non-finite semantic spaces. The technical machinery is classical: taking certainty to be Bayes-optimal accuracy and scope to be the class count n , a Fano-type argument yields a converse binding certainty and scope against mechanism capacity, with the n -ary symmetric channel attaining the exact certainty form with equality; the simplified explicit upper bound has asymptotic slack $$\ln 2/\ln n$$ on the certainty scale. Six structural extensions carry the philosophical weight. Multi-task composition compounds scope multiplicatively, so joint certainty decays as O (1/ T ); fixed-bandwidth side information yields vanishing gains; static post-processing of the mechanism’s output adds zero augmented capacity, placing chain-of-thought (so idealised) on the wrong side of the bound; sequential tool use requires logarithmically growing query counts; routing does not lift the local constraint; and context-wise feasibility need not compose into global feasibility. A synthetic bottleneck experiment illustrates the bound’s bite, with an analytical account of harder regimes via the Bhattacharyya bound. The diptych’s discrete-side engagement with Lissack, Immediato, and Watson and Sterkenburg is recorded.

title: Selective Inference for Clustering Under Unknown Covariance
abstract: Unsupervised clustering is widely used to discover underlying group structure, after which researchers often seek to validate these groups via post-hoc hypothesis testing on the population means. However, using the same data both to form clusters and to test for a difference in means inflates the Type I error rate. Recent work in selective inference has proposed solutions when the underlying data are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a known covariance matrix or an unknown isotropic covariance matrix. We propose a new selective test for the difference in means between two clusters that provably controls the Type I error rate under an arbitrary unknown covariance matrix. Our test statistic does not require estimating the feature covariance matrix; instead, it leverages a Monte Carlo sampling procedure over the set of orthogonal matrices. We show that this new selective test can be computed efficiently, and we derive closed-form solutions when clusters are formed using k-means or hierarchical clustering. In simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed p-value controls the selective Type I error rate and achieves substantial power, and we illustrate its application on gene expression and drug review data sets.

title: Deleting Code Without Losing Knowledge: Regenerative Software for Python Libraries
abstract: In the age of "Software 3.0", when a complete program can be rewritten in minutes by an agent, the traditional approach of relying on code as the sole source of truth becomes questionable. Fowler advocated for a set of seven primitives, which lay the framework for regenerative software, so that programs can be deleted and rebuilt without losing their knowledge. The knowledge lives in machine-readable records in a tracked directory, from which a *regeneration bundle* is built for each unit. The regeneration bundle is a single file with the module's architecture, intent, decisions, public contract, evaluations, and consumers, but no implementation, plus the one dependency module it may import. The open-source package spotregen implements these primitives and provides a graphical user interface. This report presents a first application of Fowler's primitives to the safety-critical forecasting library spotforecast2-safe. During the first experiments, the Claude Code session that orchestrated the study consumed more than 43 million tokens, almost all of them its own history re-sent with every request. This motivated the switch to an architecture that is built on local models. Deterministic checks and the maintainer judged the results. The report contains executable examples for every primitive. Each example runs spotregen against the repository or against a throw-away copy of it.

title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.

title: Structural Baselines Matter for Agent Failure Detection and Attribution
abstract: An LLM agent using tools can fail silently. It stops before the task is done, raises no error, and answers fluently. Two kinds of monitor address this, one deciding whether a run failed and the other naming the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model. Failing runs are longer, and the step labelled decisive is usually the last. A rule that always names the last step is correct $67\%$ to $96\%$ of the time here, without reading the run at all. That ceiling reflects how the labels were written, not how agents break. On failures whose decisive step replay can confirm, it falls to near chance. Reporting gain over that rule therefore changes what a score means. Under that correction, methods tested here gain nothing on give-up failures, while several published systems keep a clear advantage on other splits. For detection, the agent's internal states beat transcript length and text similarity on the agent benchmark, and hold up where the text baseline does not. Precision stays low when failures are rare, so such a monitor should rank runs for review, not replace it.

title: ECHO: Correcting Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts with Historical Analogues and Errors
abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide general-purpose forecasting capabilities, yet their forecasts can remain misaligned with the temporal characteristics of a target domain. This motivates lightweight forecast correction even when only black-box access to the TSFM is available. Our key observation is that two forms of historical information provide complementary correction signals: historical analogues reveal how similar contexts evolved, while past forecast errors reveal a TSFM's characteristic deviations in the target domain. Based on this observation, we propose ECHO, a black-box forecast correction framework that learns from both sources. ECHO uses AnalogE to assess retrieved historical analogues together with the current context and base forecast, learning transferable corrections through cross-domain pretraining. In parallel, RecentE learns target-specific residual corrections from past forecast errors and refines them as causally available feedback accumulates. ECHO dynamically combines the two corrections according to their observed forecasting performance. Across 5 representative TSFMs and 9 real-world datasets, ECHO reduces MSE in all 45 backbone--dataset settings, yielding an average relative reduction of 9.26\% in macro-average MSE. Its gains also extend to long-horizon forecasting.

title: Directional Pullback Regularization for Long-Horizon Rollout of Latent World Models in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Learned world models for autonomous driving operate in unconstrained latent spaces, yet the physical systems they represent are governed by strict non-holonomic constraints: ground vehicles cannot realize instantaneous pure lateral motion. We study long-horizon latent rollout modeling for autonomous driving and ask whether rollout quality can be improved by assigning a motion-aware geometry to latent transitions, rather than by redesigning the predictor architecture. Starting from an unconstrained latent rollout baseline, we introduce Directional Pullback Regularization (DPR), a training time method that defines a kinematics-aware anisotropic Riemannian metric in decoded state space and pulls it back through the decoder Jacobian to the latent manifold. The resulting latent-space metric assigns higher cost to latent directions that decode to lateral vehicle motion, while preserving the original encoder-dynamics-decoder backbone. This yields a clean three-way comparison among an Unconstrained Latent Rollout model (ULR), an Euclidean Pullback Regularization ablation (EPR), and the full directional method (DPR). We evaluate all models on open-loop ego-motion rollout over a common 10-second test horizon, using training rollout lengths of 1, 3, 5, and 10 steps. Across all four training regimes, DPR achieves lower 10-second final displacement error than both ULR and EPR. The strongest relative accuracy gain appears for models trained with 3-step rollout supervision, where DPR reduces the 10-second final displacement error by approximately 44 percent relative to ULR. The strongest overall control-relevant tradeoff is obtained for longer rollout-trained models, especially at 10 steps, where DPR simultaneously improves displacement error, lateral motion consistency, and forward motion preservation relative to both ULR and EPR.

title: Continuous-Variable Photonic Quantum Computing and Nonlinear Kerr Dynamics in Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: This work presents a high-performance, memory-safe continuous-variable (CV) photonic quantum computing simulator developed from scratch in Rust. The implementation features a rigorous 4-stage pipeline modeling initial symmetric vacuum states, single-mode squeezing, phase-space rotation, and non-Gaussian Kerr dynamics. By leveraging Rust's bare-metal execution speed and compile-time memory safety, this simulator provides a robust computational framework for investigating non-linear feature maps, phase-space deformations, and photonic architectures in Quantum Machine Learning (QML) without relying on heavy garbage collection overheads.

title: Integración de la robótica educativa para la formación vial en estudiantes del nivel primario
abstract: El presente proyecto tiene el objetivo de fomentar la educación vial por medio de la integración de la robótica educativa como estrategia innovadora en los estudiantes del Nivel Primario del Centro Educativo La Punta Pescadora. Este centro se encuentra cerca de una avenida sin medidas de seguridad vial adecuadas, por lo que se identifica esta problemática y surge la iniciativa de buscar una solución al concientizar desde edades tempranas sobre la importancia de las leyes de tránsito, mediante la creación de robots funcionales, sensores y una maqueta interactiva. Con la finalidad de desarrollar habilidades tecnológicas, conciencia vial y competencias para la vida. El tipo de estudio fue cualitativo-descriptivo, al utilizar la observación directa, la lista de cotejos y la rúbrica como técnicas de recolección de datos. La muestra estuvo conformada por 24 estudiantes seleccionados mediante muestreo intencional. Antes solo 9 (37 %) reconocían señales básicas de tránsito; después 22 (92 %) lograron identificarlas correctamente. En cuanto al uso de la robótica educativa de 24 solo 2 (8 %) la habían utilizado y al final los 24 (100 %) llegaron a familiarizarse. Los datos recolectados fueron analizados mediante categorización cualitativa, identificando patrones de participación, comprensión de normas viales y desarrollo de habilidades tecnológicas relacionadas con el uso de la robótica educativa. title: A Logarithmic Mean Optimized EfficientNet with Joint Contrastive Learning for Improving Breast Cancer Detection from Mammogram Images
abstract: Early prediction of breast cancer plays a critical role in improving patient survival rates and effective treatment planning. Mammography is the most often utilized imaging method for early breast cancer monitoring because of its ability to detect microcalcifications and subtle tissue abnormalities at an early stage. However, Mammography suffers from low sensitivity in dense breast tissue, overlapping structures and inter-observer variability, leading to high false positive rates and potential misdiagnosis. Recently, Deep Learning (DL) techniques have been utilised for mammography-based breast cancer detection, as they can automatically learn features from images. However, some models struggle with the conflation of malignant and benign areas, irrelevant feature extraction, and suboptimal training strategies. Their reliance on labelled data and classification-focused learning limits discriminative feature representation, resulting in poor differentiation of visually similar benign and malignant tissues. Hence, in this paper, an advanced DL approach is developed for efficient breast carcinoma prediction using mammography images. Initially, collected mammography images are augmented to enhance data diversity and reduce overfitting. Then, EfficientNet B7 with Joint Contrastive Learning (ENB7-JCL) is developed to learn discriminative visual representations. In ENB7-JCL, EfficientNetB7 is employed for deep feature extraction from mammography images, while JCL jointly optimizes contrastive and classification objectives by modelling similarity and dissimilarity relationships between samples. This improves the class separability and reduces misclassification of visually similar benign and malignant tissues. Additionally, the Logarithmic Mean Optimization Algorithm (LMOA) is applied to optimize the hyperparameters of EfficientNet B7 for effective training. Finally, a softmax classifier is used to perform breast cancer classification. The complete work is termed Optimized ENB7-JCL (OENB7-JCL). The experimental states that the proposed model achieves 94.85% and 95.12% of accuracy on the MIAS and INBreast dataset outperforming other existing models.
