title: Neural Processes with Normalizing Flows for Wheat Height Estimation
abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate modeling plant traits over time using neural processes, a class of machine learning models that learn distributions over functions. Plant growth is an inherently stochastic process with complex dynamics measured mostly at irregular times throughout the growing seasons. While individual trait trajectories may be simple, their distributions are shaped by complex interactions between genotype, environment, and other factors. In particular, we focus on plant height in wheat, a deceptively simple-looking trait with complex dynamics. To model these trajectory distributions, we evaluate neural processes and in particular extensions using normalizing flows, with different combinations of genotype and environmental covariates. For controlled evaluations, we generate synthetic wheat height trajectories calibrated against Swiss weather station records and the Field Phenotyping Platform 1.0 (FIP1) wheat dataset. To fully evaluate these trajectory distributions, we use signatures, vector representations of sequential data, together with the signature maximum mean discrepancy (Sig-MMD) and its recently introduced censored variant (CSig-MMD). Sig-MMD enables direct pathwise comparison of predicted and simulator trajectory distributions, while CSig-MMD focuses this comparison on the tail, including lodged trajectories. Together, these metrics allow us to assess whether the models capture the full distribution of growth trajectories, including rare outcomes. We compare the neural processes with a lodging-mixture spline baseline and apply them to the FIP1 data.

title: CTIA: Explainable and Adaptive Probability Assignment for Cryptographic Micropayment Tickets
abstract: In digital systems, micropayments refer to extremely small transactions which occur frequently. These micropayments support a lot of existing systems such as pay-per-API billing, machine-to-machine interaction, and incentive mechanisms in distributed networks. Probabilistic micropayment systems enhance the system, by settling only a subset of transfers, although the rules for these probability are either prefixed or purely cryptographic. Due to this the system loses governance and limits auditability, and leaves with no explanation of the final win/lose outcome. This paper introduces CTIA (Cryptographic Ticket Issuer Agent), focused on a decision-layer component that assigns per-ticket win probabilities from telemetry while leaving the cryptographic ticket format and deterministic lottery verification unchanged. CTIA uses a Random Forest regressor to map telemetry (network load, relay reputation, budget utilization, and recent win rate) to a probability p , and logs SHAP attributions per issuance as an auditable explanation log. We evaluated CTIA under low-probability micropayment regimes under controlled simulations and compared it to static, analytic and alternative machine-learning controllers. With the results we found that CTIA preserves the intended probability and payout scale while providing adaptive and auditable probability assignments. However we noticed that fairness outcomes varied across regimes and were not consistently better than simpler controllers. During the experiment, we also observed that adaptive probability assignment can affect participant-level and temporal reward distribution, but the magnitude and direction of the effect were dependent on the probability regime, controller and evaluation horizon. Thus though this study we would like to position CTIA as an auditable probability-assignment layer.

title: Making Tensor Decoupling More Robust and Less Parametric
abstract: Tensor decoupling algorithms recover compact representations of multivariate functions by combining linear factor matrices with univariate internal nonlinearities. We identify two limitations of recent methods. First, their performance is not invariant to mismatched output or gradient magnitudes, and second, their spline internals require manual tuning of their degrees of freedom. We propose two lightweight fixes. The first is a preprocessing step that rescales the input Jacobian tensor, removing both the bias towards larger magnitude outputs and the ill-conditioning of certain factor updates caused by such a mismatch. The second replaces B-spline internals by penalized splines coupled with generalized cross-validation, making the method less dependent on the user selecting the right number of control points. Finally, we release an efficient open-source JAX implementation of our algorithm.

title: Taming Nonconvexity with Epigraph Lifting
abstract: We consider inverse problems regularized by a trained neural network with \emph{convex activations} and \emph{unrestricted weights}. The resulting optimization problem is generally nonconvex, and gradient-based methods may converge to poor local minima. We introduce a \emph{penalized epigraph lifting} of the network and show that the lifted problem admits a \emph{difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition}. For Lipschitz continuous activations, we establish \emph{finite exactness}: the original objective is recovered exactly at a finite and explicitly computable penalty threshold $\barρ$. Building on this structure, we propose \emph{H-DC} (Homotopic DC), a homotopic scheme that solves a sequence of DC subproblems with increasing $ρ$, warm-starting each level from the previous solution. Numerical experiments on synthetic problems, a manifold denoiser regularizer, and image inpainting with a learned Mumford--Shah regularizer show that H-DC consistently escapes poor local minima and reaches solutions with lower objective values than gradient-based methods from the same initialization.

title: CIPHEUR: LLM-Guided Structural Search Control for Conflict-Graph Optimization
abstract: Conflict-graph search can stagnate despite effective operators when interventions fail to address the conflicts blocking progress. A disruptive intervention may also require further search before its value emerges. We propose CIPHEUR, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that connects conflict evidence to coordinated intervention and recovery through Structured Intervention Units (SIUs). The shared control interface supports offline synthesis of executable policies and online contextual decisions. Asynchronous online control sustains native search during inference, while all policies preserve the original objective and feasibility constraints. Across eight satellite-ground scheduling conflict views with five runs per view and a 900-second evaluation cap, CIPHEUR-online achieves the highest mean objective among 11 configurations and increases mean scheduled contact duration by 14.84% over the greedy baseline GWMIN. It exceeds the strongest external per-view mean in seven of eight views and outperforms CHILS in all 40 paired runs. Within the same runs, its normalized objective improvement from 360 to 900 seconds is 1.50 to 1.86 times that of the two programmatic controllers. A separately frozen, one-shot LLM-generated controller also improves the mean objective over CHILS without runtime model calls. Together, these results demonstrate how structural search control translates LLM design knowledge and contextual reasoning into improved solution quality and sustained search progress.

title: The Impact of Imperfect XAI on Human-AI Decision-Making
abstract: Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

title: Code and experiment logs for "Closed-form signed Hessian blocks in bilinear neural parameterisations"
abstract: Code, scripts and run logs accompanying the manuscript “Closed-form signed Hessian blocks in bilinear neural parameterisations” (V. Oban, submitted to Neural Networks). The archive contains (i) JAX scripts for the exact-Hessian experiments: verification of the factorisation-induced curvature, escape-time and weight-decay threshold tests, the small causal transformer, the general bilinear structures (attention, normalisation gains, ResNet-20), nearly dead slots, sign-descent escape and trapping, and the critical-boundary (fourth-order) tests; (ii) PyTorch/Kaggle notebooks for the RoBERTa-base LoRA experiments on MRPC and RTE; and (iii) the JSON logs of every run reported in the paper. All synthetic data are generated by the scripts; the public datasets used are listed in the README.

title: User-Directed Orchestration in Modular AI Architectures: Separation of Specialization and Character
abstract: This article proposes the manual orchestration of a modular AI architecture in which domain specialization and a user-selected persona (character) are treated as independent control parameters. The user selects the specialization responsible for solving a task and the character that frames the final response. A specialist model serves as the primary domain-competence center within its module. An Arbiter evaluates candidate outputs, determines whether they may be released, and applies the selected character within the permissions defined for the module. Character is a framing function rather than a general-purpose content-rewriting mechanism. It may shape the opening, closing, and other designated elements of an answer while preserving the specialist's substantive contribution. The extent of the Arbiter's authority to revise content depends on the module's defined responsibilities and constraints. Some modules may permit substantive revision, while others may restrict the Arbiter to admissibility checks and character application. The architecture also proposes an optional task-agent layer within specialist modules. Users may create agents with different professional profiles based on the module's underlying model, allowing differentiated work within one module without necessarily invoking additional models. Agents may execute bounded subtasks, such as checking calculations, comparing scenarios, extracting information, or conducting preliminary document screening. Their use is conditional on task requirements; they are not a mandatory layer and do not replace the specialist model's domain competence. The Selector supports user-directed configuration, including individual specializations, composite configurations, and changes of specialization during an ongoing dialogue. A user may request a second specialist to review a previous answer without requiring multiple specialist models to run on the original request. The Arbiter remains responsible for the final release decision, including when additional resources or verification procedures are used. The proposal distinguishes user-directed selection, domain-level reasoning, task-level execution, output arbitration, and user-directed transitions between specialists. It is a conceptual architecture intended to guide implementation and empirical evaluation.

title: Unlocking User-Generated Content for Academic Library Service Quality Assessment: A Multidimensional Text Analytics Framework
abstract: While traditional metrics and survey-based models such as LibQUAL+ grant valuable foundations for evaluating academic library service quality, they may not fully capture the immediacy and nuance of evolving patron experiences. As libraries increasingly become interactive community hubs, User-Generated Content, including Google reviews, provides a rich, authentic source of unfiltered feedback. Recognizing both the scalability obstacles of manual coding and the semantic limitations of conventional probabilistic models, this study puts forward a multidimensional text analytics framework designed to bridge these gaps with precision and sensitivity to user voices. Examining 8542 multilingual Google reviews from 88 academic libraries across a broad, multinational sample, this approach adopts a Zero-Shot Classification pipeline for theoretically anchored thematic categories with a rating-fortified VADER sentiment analysis to capture delicate emotional dimensions. Findings highlight a clear distribution of thematic feedback. While physical spaces and community events generate the highest satisfaction, digital infrastructure and staff interactions are identified as primary operational challenges. Finally, this data-driven framework seeks to transform unstructured UGC into actionable intelligence, supporting library administrators in making dynamic, evidence-based decisions that respond to the genuine needs and lived experiences of their communities.

title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

title: Size Generalization for Diffusion Routing Solvers
abstract: Routing problems, like the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), are NP-hard and slow to solve for large instances. Diffusion-based solvers can be trained in a supervised way using sets of optimal solutions, and then quickly solve new test instances. However, for large instances, optimal solutions are hard to find, and diffusion models fail to generalize to instance sizes outside their training distribution. Here we describe ResizeCO, a label free size-generalization approach that addresses both the change in statistical properties of larger instances, and the computational challenge of solving them quickly. It uses reinforcement learning on large-scale instances to adapt a diffusion model trained on small instances. Specifically, we adapt GRPO to this problem, using route length as the training signal. ResizeCO also formulates k-opt as a tree search, solved by a beam search on the GPU. In size-generalization experiments on TSP and CVRP instances with up to 10000 nodes, ResizeCO achieves a Pareto front over route quality and time that dominates learned solvers, and also outperforms other solvers at short run times, setting a new state of the art.

title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.

title: RFWeave: Learning Wireless Propagation Across Scenes and Transceiver Configurations
abstract: Wireless propagation modeling is foundational to the evaluation and design of modern communication systems. To achieve accurate wireless propagation prediction, recent learning-based approaches leverage scene geometry and materials, demonstrating promising generalization across transceiver locations and unseen scenes. However, these approaches remain largely confined to a fixed configuration of array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. In this work, we introduce RFWeave, a learned wireless propagation model designed to generalize across scenes, transceiver locations, and transceiver configurations. To accommodate varying array structures, RFWeave incorporates variable-length transceiver tokens that represent antenna elements individually. Furthermore, to capture the geometry between transmit and receive antenna elements, RFWeave aggregates their pairwise spatial relations into propagation tokens. A configuration-conditioned decoder predicts the spatial spectrum and received power. RFWeave is trained on a large-scale simulated dataset spanning 10,000 indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records under diverse transceiver configurations. Extensive evaluations show that RFWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated generalization settings, improving spatial spectrum structural similarity (SSIM) by up to 15.7% and reducing received power mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 35.4% over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes. Additional experiments on measured DICHASUS data and in beam management further demonstrate RFWeave's broader applicability to real-world channels and downstream wireless tasks.

title: Collective Floquet engineering between two distant superconducting artificial atoms
abstract: A one-dimensional waveguide is a crucial medium for transferring propagating quantum information between remote qubits, yet the photon-mediated interaction is typically fixed by the static device geometry, qubit parameters, and their couplings to the transmission line. Such an interaction can be engineered to be coherent or dissipative via virtual- or real-photon exchange, respectively, yet its effective strength remains fixed in either case. Here we demonstrate dynamical control over this interaction by applying Floquet engineering to two superconducting qubits coupled to a waveguide terminated by a capacitive mirror. By positioning one qubit at an antinode and the other qubit at a node or an antinode of the resonant standing wave, we realize a Hermitian or non-Hermitian coupling between the two qubits. A periodic flux drive of the qubit frequencies then enables on-demand control of the coherent energy splitting and the collective decay. Our results establish Floquet engineering as a route to dynamically reshape both coherent and dissipative photon-mediated interactions between remote quantum emitters.

title: Deterministic preparation of squeezed and non-Gaussian states in coupled qubit-boson systems
abstract: Deterministic preparation of bosonic resource states is a central task in continuous-variable quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Here we develop a measurement-based imaginary time evolution (MITE) protocol for preparing squeezed and non-Gaussian states. The protocol combines ancilla-mediated weak measurements of the Hamiltonian with a conditional phase rotation that suppresses excited state trapping and stabilizes convergence toward the ground state. The method is potentially applicable in hybrid discrete variable-continuous variable (DV-CV) platforms, where the qubit acts as the measurement readout. We demonstrate deterministic convergence over a broad range of parameters and show that the performance degradation near the stability boundary is governed by the shrinking Bogoliubov quasiparticle gap. The same framework also extends to non-Gaussian bosonic resource states, including Schrödinger cat states and excited states of the single-mode squeezing Hamiltonian, which display Wigner negativity. The squeezed states remain robust under bosonic loss over experimentally relevant regimes.

title: Benchmarking and Evaluating Frontier Models
abstract: This dataset supports a practical demonstration of persona adaptation and safety steering in Gemma 2, comparing a base model with an adapted model through recorded responses, evaluation scores, and activation summaries. The portable demo_data.tar archive contains everything needed to replay four demonstration phases: Baseline: 208 paired turns with persona-adherence scores. JBDistill-Bench: 500 paired prompts with safety judgments. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA): activation-pattern comparisons and separately tested steering at layers 14 and 20. Steered: 180 recorded before/after comparisons across both models. The archive includes the demonstration interface, compact playback data, a local server, the frozen safety report, usage instructions, and checksums. Playback requires no GPU, model download, credentials, or new inference calls. DEMO_DATA.md explains installation, metrics, sample counts, and limitations. Persona adherence and safety are evaluated separately. Steered results cover selected matched subsets rather than a repeat of the full benchmark. Activation patterns describe associations and do not establish causal importance. Additional files contain selected activation evidence and transfer manifests. The portable archive reproduces the saved demonstration; it does not contain every raw activation capture or all artifacts required to retrain the models. Only complete, checksum-verified archive sets should be used.

title: Generative AI-Based Framework for Automated Knowledge Discovery from Unstructured Data
abstract: The rapid rise of unstructured text data in various scientific, technical and corporate contexts is driving the necessity for automated tools to distill usable knowledge from this raw text without extensive curatorial effort. In this paper we introduce a framework which uses generative AI techniques to convert unstructured documents into structured knowledge bases that can be queried using a pipeline of large language models combined with ontology-based extraction, entity canonicalization and retrieval-augmented generation. Our architecture solves three recurring problems of knowledge discovery: extraction hallucinations, entity fragmentation and lack of alignment between queries and evidence in extracted knowledge. Our framework uses a two-step extraction approach that distinguishes between candidate generation and structural validation, with an identity resolution component that unifies various forms of surface-level entities into canonical entities. Experimentally, on a wide range of heterogeneous corpora, we show that our framework greatly mitigates noise introduced by node generation from unstructured documents, improves consistency of entity resolution and enables multi-hop querying over document-driven knowledge structures.

title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

title: Perfect discrimination of an orthogonal $2\otimes2$ basis may require collective separable measurements on two copies
abstract: We consider an orthogonal basis of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$ with three entangled states and one product state. This basis is not perfectly distinguishable by LOCC or even by separable measurements when a single copy of the unknown state is available. We show that with two copies no adaptive separable protocol, which measures the copies one at a time, distinguishes the basis perfectly. We then show that a collective separable measurement on the two copies does. Whether two copies suffice for LOCC remains open.

title: From equations to prompts: integrating LLMs into a hybrid macroeconomic ABM
abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) typically rely on equations to incorporate agents' decision-making, ranging from ad-hoc rules or simple heuristics to complex, theory- or data-driven approaches. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) make it possible to represent economic decision-making through information-conditioned decisions rather than explicitly specified behavioural equations. However, whether LLM-driven agents can feasibly replace individual components in an ABM and the degree to which they can replicate observed economic dynamics remains insufficiently understood. In particular, it is unclear whether the integration of LLM-driven agents in a macroeconomic ABM can generate historically plausible macroeconomic trajectories and how their performance depends on the information provided to them and on the scale of the underlying model. This paper addresses these questions by introducing an LLM-driven bank agent into a data-driven macroeconomic model of the Greek economy, where it determines consumer credit and lending rates. Results show that the LLM-driven agent's decisions can reproduce historical consumer credit dynamics relatively well, although their performance in replicating lending rates is weaker and more heterogeneous; broader economic information generally improves performance, while larger models do not systematically outperform smaller ones. Overall, the study provides encouraging evidence that LLM-driven agents can be feasibly integrated into macroeconomic ABMs, assimilating economically relevant information and producing outcomes that closely match observed data, without requiring explicit functional forms for behavioural relationships - pointing towards the possibility of enabling economic simulations to shift from equations to prompts.

title: Corrigendum to: Artificial Intelligence in Cancer Diagnosis: A Game-changer in Healthcare
abstract: Following publication of the article entitled "Artificial Intelligence in Cancer Diagnosis: A Game-changer in Healthcare" [1], certain phrases and expressions were identified that were unclear or inconsistent with established scientific terminology. To ensure the accuracy and clarity of the published record, these expressions have been corrected using appropriate terminology that more accurately conveys the intended scientific meaning. These corrections are limited to the wording and terminology of the affected passages and do not alter the data, results, scientific interpretations, or conclusions of the article. The specific corrections are provided below: 4.1. title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence-based and pathologist scoring of murine bile duct hyperplasia
abstract: Bile duct hyperplasia in rodents, caused by chemical cytotoxicity, bile flow interference, or aging, is traditionally assessed through time-consuming microscopic examination by pathologists. We developed a deep learning-based, artificial intelligence (AI) model for quick and accurate assessment of bile duct hyperplasia in mice. The study utilized 127 hematoxylin and eosin-stained, mouse liver whole-slide images (WSIs) digitized using Aperio scanners. A segmentation algorithm with a U-Net architecture and an EfficientNet backbone was trained on 1165 areas from 35 WSIs to identify and quantify bile ducts, measure their area percentage using a supervised method, and categorize them into grades 0 to 4 using an unsupervised method. The model was validated on 24 WSIs and tested on 68 WSIs, all independently scored by 3 veterinary pathologists using consensus criteria. The segmentation model achieved Dice scores of 91.75% in training and 85.88% in validation. Testing revealed high sensitivity (95%), specificity (97%), and Dice score (95.45%), indicating robust model accuracy. Model-predicted grades showed strong correlation ( r 2 s = 0.86) with pathologists’ consensus scores. This AI-driven approach has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of bile duct hyperplasia assessments in rodent studies, paving the way for more standardized, objective, and high-throughput histological evaluations in preclinical research.

title: Domain adaptation affects adversarial robustness in autonomous steering models
abstract: Abstract Domain adaptation is commonly used to transfer autonomous steering models across regions with different road configurations, such as from right-hand to left-hand traffic. While prior work has largely evaluated adaptation using clean target-domain steering accuracy, its effect on adversarial robustness remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates two steering architectures, PilotNet and ResNet-18, under four adaptation strategies: U.S.-trained, flipped U.S.-trained, U.S.-trained + fine-tuned, and flipped U.S.-trained + fine-tuned. Robustness is assessed under FGSM and PGD attacks across multiple perturbation levels using normalized robustness scores and absolute steering-error metrics. Results show that domain adaptation improves clean target-domain accuracy but affects adversarial robustness in a metric-dependent manner. Fine-tuned models often show degraded normalized adversarial robustness, especially after flipped pretraining, indicating larger relative sensitivity to adversarial perturbations compared with their clean baselines. However, absolute adversarial errors show that fine-tuned models are not always worse than pretrained baselines under attack. These results show that, after domain adaptation, clean accuracy and normalized robustness can diverge, and RS may rank robustness differently from absolute steering-error metrics when clean baselines differ. The contribution of this study is to show that metric choice materially affects robustness conclusions for domain-adapted steering models; therefore, RS remains useful for measuring relative degradation, but should be interpreted alongside absolute steering-error metrics and statistical uncertainty.

title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations
abstract: Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs) aim to capture clinically useful information beyond sleep staging, yet are rarely compared with sleep-staging encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage. Using a common whole-night, missingness-aware state-space downstream modeling framework, we compared frozen representations from prominent large-scale, multi-cohort sleep-stage-supervised encoders and self-supervised PSG FMs for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups in 7,906 PSGs from an unseen registry. Although PSG FMs outperformed an EEG-only, single-cohort supervised baseline, this ordering reversed when supervised pretraining approached comparable scale and modality coverage. Transfer learning from neural sleep scorers achieved higher overall performance while exhibiting greater downstream data efficiency. These findings underscore the need for scale- and modality-matched pretrained supervised baselines when assessing PSG FMs' downstream potential.

title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.

title: Guidance Without Labels: Flow Matching from Coupled Gaussian Mixtures
abstract: Flow matching models are typically trained to transport a Gaussian source to the data distribution, with source and target samples paired independently. We replace the source with a fitted Gaussian mixture and couple each data point to a mixture component through an entropic optimal transport problem. We show that the resulting transport reduces to the standard Gaussian-source problem up to a guidance-like correction, which enables the reuse of a pretrained velocity field. This correction is a closed-form function of the fitted mixture plus a term that we learn with a small correction network. We test our model on published checkpoints for CIFAR-10 and CelebA-HQ. It improves FID at every step count, and on CelebA-HQ it reaches the quality of the baseline with about half the steps. The closed-form term alone, with no training, already delivers most of this improvement; the small correction network accounts for the rest.

title: Learning Rules, Memorizing Facts: An Information-Theoretic View of Hallucination
abstract: Understanding the relationship between generalization and hallucination requires clarifying the role of memorization. We study this relationship from an information-theoretic perspective through a Selector-Density Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework. In the sparse random-fact limit, a uniformly bounded information budget per fact forces a nonvanishing false-positive rate at recall bounded away from zero, even when all facts are observed during training. In a rules-and-facts setting, we decompose model-data mutual information into rule learning, atomic-fact memory, and excess memorization, revealing competition between rule learning and factual memory even without excess memorization. A joint budget bound quantifies the resulting constraint on atomic hallucination under perfect atomic recall. Moreover, an additive Gaussian model shows that maintaining high recall for atomic and composite facts incurs false positives even under optimal data mixing. Finally, controlled relational experiments hint how training exposure, rule complexity, and model capacity shape these trade-offs.

title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions
abstract: Learning equilibria from data is difficult when several decision makers interact indefinitely and the system state has no prescribed bounds. We examine discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian transition noise. The proposed procedure uses a single uninterrupted trajectory to update Gaussian-process models of the drift and to solve successively refined finite games. We prove a perturbation result showing that stability of equilibrium selection, together with uniform KL accuracy of Gaussian transition models, is sufficient for regional uniform convergence of the induced values and approximate Nash behavior in the original game. The region specifies where the guarantees are evaluated; strategies and dynamics continue to act on the entire Euclidean state space. For GP estimators, simultaneous confidence bounds yield a rate controlled by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension. Numerical studies illustrate how kernel choice and dimension appear in the predicted convergence behavior.

title: A Machine Learning-Based Platform for Sentiment Analysis of Movie Reviews
abstract: Sentiment analysis is the computational study of opinions and attitudes expressed in text. With the rapid growth of online reviews, especially in the film industry, it has become increasingly difficult to process user-generated content for decision-making. This study presents a sentiment analysis management platform designed to classify and visualize user opinions on movie reviews. A Facebook page was created to collect 25,000 comments from 20 adventure films, which served as the dataset. Using Python, the system implemented supervised and unsupervised learning approaches, with logistic regression and support vector machines tested against existing movie review corpora. Classification was performed on the basis of subjectivity and polarity, producing visual outputs to support fast decision-making. Experimental results demonstrated a classification accuracy of 88.1 percent, indicating the effectiveness of the platform in managing large-scale opinion data.

title: Resource-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Compact LLMs for Supply Chain Operations: A Hybrid QLoRA and RAG Approach
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer transformative potential for enterprise automation, particularly within the highly complex and data-dense environments of transportation, supply chain management, and intralogistics. However, deploying foundational models in these specialized domains frequently results in a critical failure mode: confident generative hallucinations regarding company-specific, highly proprietary operational protocols. Furthermore, adapting these massive models typically requires prohibitive computational resources, placing them fundamentally out of reach for regional distribution hubs and mid-sized enterprises constrained by strict hardware budgets. This paper investigates the hypothesis that a compact, instruction-tuned Small Language Model (SLM) can be aggressively fine-tuned and semantically grounded to provide highly accurate, factually bound supply chain support while operating entirely within the constraints of a single commodity GPU. This research presents the end-to-end development, optimization, and deployment of IndustryGPT, a highly specialized logistics LLM. We utilize a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy, specifically 4-bit Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA), to adapt the 1.1-billion parameter TinyLlama base model using a single 16 GB NVIDIA T4 GPU. To systematically eliminate hallucinations and ground the model in factual warehouse operations, we introduce a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture powered by a local FAISS vector database. This hybrid pipeline dynamically retrieves and injects exact standard operating procedures (SOPs) such as inbound packet scanning workflows, tallying reconciliations, and strict fleet maintenance protocols directly into the inference context window. We evaluate the model's performance on a custom hybrid corpus merging customer support dialogues with synthetic routing data, reporting substantial gains in both structural coherence and factual adherence. The system successfully demonstrates that merging domain-specific supervised fine-tuning with dense vector retrieval allows lightweight, edge-deployed models to achieve enterprise-grade accuracy. Finally, the architecture is deployed via a Gradio web interface, providing an interactive, zero-hallucination conversational agent tailored for localized logistics exception handling, proving that data sovereignty and advanced AI automation can coexist on localized commodity hardware.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Imbalanced Financial Classification and Its Societal Implications for Digital Trust: A Cost-Sensitive XGBoost–Transformer Ensemble
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates how financial institutions decide who is trusted, who is scrutinised, and who is refused — decisions that carry direct social consequences for individuals and communities. Automated credit-risk and fraud-assessment systems are deployed at a scale where their errors are not merely statistical but socially consequential, because they can restrict access to credit, widen financial exclusion, and erode public confidence in digital finance. This paper addresses one technical precondition for trustworthy deployment: reliable learning from severely imbalanced financial data. It treats the task as what the data actually measure — prediction of credit-card default rather than verified fraud — and proposes FraudShield, a hybrid framework that combines a gradient-boosting model (XGBoost), a Transformer-based tabular model, an adaptive gating mechanism that learns a per-instance weighting of the two branches, and a cost-sensitive decision layer that reflects the unequal social and economic cost of different errors. The framework is evaluated on the UCI Credit Card Default dataset (30,000 clients), whose positive (default) class comprises 22.12% of the observations — a ratio of approximately 1:3.52. The evaluation protocol splits the data before any preprocessing, fits target encoding and standardization within each training fold only, and applies SMOTE to the training folds alone. Under this corrected protocol, FraudShield attains an AUC-ROC of 0.943 and an F1-score of 0.892, and the cost-sensitive layer raises measured cost savings from 16.7% to 28.4% over the majority-class baseline. The paper interprets these results within a broader discussion of AI accountability, fairness, and digital trust, and argues that technically sound imbalanced-learning methods are a necessary — though not sufficient — condition for socially responsible automated decision-making in finance.

title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
abstract: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.

title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. title: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT
abstract: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and inefficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full-sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset-coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative relaxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propagation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential trajectory in parallel. By exploiting the lower bidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formulates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an $O(\log T)$ temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below $10^{-7}$ relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Triton implementation delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four sequential classification benchmarks. By reconciling parallel training with step-by-step execution, FidLIF enables high-fidelity spiking dynamics to benefit from parallel hardware without compromising incremental inference at deployment.

title: Learning $ω$-Powered Conditional Distributions with Importance-Weighted Flow Matching
abstract: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) with guidance scale $γ$ is commonly motivated by the $ω$-powered conditional distribution obtained by setting $ω=γ$, but CFG does not, in general, sample from this distribution exactly. We study whether the powered target can instead be learned explicitly. We introduce Importance-Weighted Conditional Flow Matching (IW-CFM), which reweights conditional flow-matching examples using density ratios obtained from frozen conditional and unconditional flow models. With exact normalized weights, the resulting objective has the same gradient as flow matching on the powered target; in practice, we use self-normalized estimation and a regularized empirical approximation for high-dimensional data. On synthetic distributions, IW-CFM recovers analytical powered targets for which numerically matched CFG, $γ=ω$, exhibits a visible mismatch. On ImageNet, an amortized lightweight corrector achieves better alignment than fixed- and matched-guidance CFG with the corresponding weighted and filtered reference distributions. We additionally present an exploratory CLIP analysis of powered-density rankings on real ImageNet data. Aggregate shifts across selected prompt-specific contrasts coexist with heterogeneous classwise responses, including nonmonotonic trajectories. These results provide a practical route for studying and approximating model-defined powered conditional distributions.

title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.

title: Prospects for Using Information Dialectics to Improve AI: The Concept of Galois-Field-Based Intrinsic Explainability
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence in recent years has been driven primarily by engineering advances, while the philosophical foundations of the concept of “intelligence” itself have been reconsidered much more slowly. This paper proposes a conceptual research program based on the thesis that philosophical analysis can serve not only as a means of interpreting existing technologies but also as a source of architectural principles for artificial intelligence. The main thesis of the paper is that an artificial system that aspires to functionally approximate human conceptual thinking must not only statistically process natural language utterances but also adequately interpret the place of the concepts used within the structure of natural language. Specifically, the meaning of fundamental concepts should be determined through their interrelations with one another, rather than through a set of vocabulary features. The simplest example of such an interrelation is the opposition through which paired philosophical categories are defined in objective dialectic. A dialectical concept of information is used as a substantive example. This concept, based on the basic opposition between the categories of “matter” and “information,” constructs derivative concepts (“alienated information,” “signal,” etc.). The work builds on the existing relational bottleneck paradigm. The distinctive feature of the proposed approach lies in its transfer of the bottleneck to semantically interpretable relations between concepts and the requirement that this layer be computationally sufficient to obtain the result. On this basis, the concept of Galois-field-based intrinsic explainability (GFIE) is proposed. Galois fields are viewed not as a natural “algebra of meaning,” but as a potential computational substrate for the implementation of predefined finite semantic operations. A minimal proof-of-constructibility is provided: a three-valued semantic operation is first defined independently, then encoded in GF(3) and implemented by a polynomial function. This example demonstrates the “semantics first, algebra second” principle, excluding the direct attribution of meaningful meaning to the addition or multiplication of field elements. This paper presents a conceptual framework and research program, not a report on a constructed and empirically validated AI architecture. Existing results in the algebraization of multivalued operations, finite-field computations, partial digital convolutions, and modular computing architectures are considered as individual, potentially applicable components, but not as proof of a complete technical implementation of GFIE.

title: Применение больших языковых моделей (LLM) в психологии
abstract: В статье рассматривается потенциал использования в психологической науке и практике больших языковых моделей (LLM) как инструмента для когнитивных исследований и как квазисубъекта оказания консультационной поддержки. Производится анализ особенностей применения и причин ограничений, в том числе анализ когнитивных особенностей LLM и архитектурных механизмов их формирования. Процессы обработки и преобразования векторных представлений в больших языковых моделях могут оказаться полезными для изучения механизмов человеческого довербального мышления и, возможно, для понимания человеческих речевых дисфункций. Несмотря на отсутствие сенсорного (телесного) опыта и подлинной эмпатии, языковые модели демонстрируют квазипсихологические феномены (подобие этики), сформированные на основе статистических предпочтений. Модели также обладают способностью идентификации себя, что является свойством конструкта сознания. Анализируется, какие именно ограничения использования являются существенными и непреодолимыми для существующей архитектуры LLM. Ограничения рассматриваются в том числе на примере эмпирических эмуляций длительных психотерапевтических сессий. Установлено, что современные языковые модели LLM могут быть полезны в задачах когнитивного рефрейминга (как зеркало для экстернализации проблем), при этом в ситуации психологической уязвимости пользователя возможность ошибок, присущих архитектуре LLM, таких как выстраивание правдоподобных, но неверных и не подкрепленных эмпатией интерпретаций, представляет опасность. Кроме того, установлено, что LLM фундаментально непригодны для полноценной психотерапии вследствие дискретности процесса генерации ответов, вероятностного механизма внимания, отсутствия адекватной оценки качества предлагаемых решений, а также в силу отсутствия метакогниции. В статье достигнуты цели определения особенностей и ограничений применения больших языковых моделей (LLM) в психологии путем детального анализа их архитектурных особенностей и недостатков.

title: Using Nav-Mesh Flood Fill to Speed Up Environment Querying
abstract: In almost every game, you need to query the environment for positions and objects for your agents. The most common attribute for these queries is distance. In complex environments, pathfinding data from nav-mesh are more accurate than basic distance checks. They can help you filter out unreachable positions or give distances through obstacles. However, calculating paths for every possible position is slow. Especially when multiple agents are requesting at the same time. To face this problem, we decided to run the flood-fill algorithm through nav-mesh faces. It allows us to pre-calculate pathfinding data for selected areas and reuse it for multiple queries. This technique allows to increase the number of positions taken into consideration, leading to more optimal results.

title: Mapping the discourse on neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury: A signal-generation natural language processing study of Reddit communities
abstract: STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional natural language processing (NLP) study of publicly available Reddit data. OBJECTIVES: To map the thematic structure and affective tone of neuropathic pain discourse among Reddit users self-identifying with spinal cord injury (SCI) or clinically overlapping cord and cauda pathology, and to surface candidate hypotheses for triangulation with patient-reported and clinical data. SETTING: Public Reddit communities. METHODS: Searches across ten subreddits using twenty query strings yielded 1489 candidate posts. A two-tier keyword filter (SCI-spectrum population term plus a pain or treatment term) retained 517 unique documents from six communities. Documents were embedded with a sentence-transformer model, reduced with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and clustered using KMeans (K = 10) within a BERTopic representation pipeline, with the cluster count and cluster labels informed by a lexically derived seed-topic list. Cluster stability and sensitivity to the choice of K were assessed. Themes were characterised by class-term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) keywords and provisional large language model labelling. Sentiment was assigned using a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned on social media text; because the classifier was not calibrated in this clinical domain, sentiment proportions are reported as directional, ordinal signals rather than calibrated estimates. Engagement was operationalised as median upvote score and comment count per theme. RESULTS: The corpus was dominated by r/spinalcordinjuries (41%) and r/ChronicPain (23%). Overall sentiment was negative in 56.1% of posts (uncalibrated). Ten interpretable themes were identified within this two-community corpus. The highest negative-sentiment shares were in Treatment-Refractory Pain and Psychological Burden, Opioid and Polypharmacy Management Challenges, and Severe Spasticity Progression; the lowest were in Spinal Cord Stimulation Devices and Advanced Neuromodulation. Engagement was highest for crisis narratives (median upvote score 13) and opioid-management discourse (median 22 comments). CONCLUSIONS: Within the sampled Reddit communities, discourse on neuropathic pain in SCI and overlapping cord/cauda pathology is dominated by negative affect, treatment refractoriness, and psychosocial burden, while emerging neuromodulation themes attract comparatively less negative sentiment. Findings are signal-generating, require triangulation with clinical data, and should not be read as representative of the broader SCI population. SPONSORSHIP: None.

title: SMOTE extensions for abnormal minority instances in imbalanced time series classification
abstract: Abstract Class imbalance remains a significant challenge in time series classification, especially when the minority samples include abnormal or outlier instances. This study proposes four extensions of the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE): Distance Extended SMOTE, Dirichlet Extended SMOTE, Feature-Correlation and Random-Perturbation SMOTE, and Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model (BGMM) SMOTE. These methods use weighted neighbor selection, probabilistic modeling, and clustering to generate synthetic samples. Augmentation was applied only to the training data after train–test splitting and within the validation process, while the test data remained unseen. The proposed methods were integrated with a Bayesian Deep Bidirectional LSTM classifier using Monte Carlo dropout-based variational inference to enable both robust classification and uncertainty quantification. Experiments on five benchmark time-series datasets showed that based on stratified 10-fold cross-validation, the proposed SMOTE extensions consistently surpassed baseline methods and standard SMOTE. BGMM-SMOTE and Dirichlet Extended SMOTE achieved the best performance. The present study gives a detailed analysis of SMOTE enhancements specifically designed for abnormal class distributions, providing an appropriate method to handle imbalanced time series classification. The framework combines advanced resampling methods with Bayesian deep learning to make more reliable predictions, with applications in healthcare monitoring, fault detection, and other safety-critical fields.

title: TableVision: Recovering Verified Structure from Historical Tables
abstract: Gaps, skips, and mistakes are the normal state of a historical register: rows go missing, tables cross page breaks, columns slip under wrong names, and column sums disagree with the corresponding row entries. Readers read digits correctly but lose the table structure. On seven clean panels of election returns, the best open-source reader reproduces 99.0\% of the digits but files only 83.7\% of the figures in the correct cells and gets 11 of 30 columns correct. TableVision treats table structure recovery as the problem. On three degraded 1888 pages, Amazon Textract files only 1 of 1494 figures correctly; TableVision correctly files 99.2\%, and all 51 columns its exact-total check releases are correct. A dynamic program cuts a volume into blocks by how many columns sum to their last line; witnesses read the cells; the gate classifies each column as exactly reconciling, flagged as faithful to a page whose arithmetic is wrong, or withheld. A theory of the sum check says which errors it cannot see and why its optimal block is about $θ^{-1/2}$ rows at defect rate $θ$. On 2201 columns of Wisconsin electoral data, the gate accepts 2042, flags 118, and withholds 41; failure rises with column length $R$ as $1-(1-θ)^R$ at 1.1 defects per 1000 cells in general elections; official returns confirm 933 of 934 testable accepted sums and all 35 testable flagged totals; and the deployment added 491\,359 gated precinct rows to a 9.3-million-row dataset. One implication is that the design of the verification block is critical.

title: Not All Challenges Are Equal: Evaluating Interactive Liveness Detection Against Real-Time Face Swaps
abstract: Remote identity verification assumes that a camera stream shows a live person, yet public real-time face-swap tools can replace that person before the stream reaches the verifier. Passive deepfake detectors generalize poorly to new generators, while interactive challenges are often selected without evidence of which gestures expose current attacks. We evaluate randomized gesture challenges in 108 live sessions with six subjects, 24 impersonated identities, and two face-swap tools, DeepFaceLive and FaceFusion, injected through a virtual camera. The static calibration segment reaches a session-level AUC of 0.878 with a frozen UCF spatial detector, while the mean across the active-gesture windows reaches 0.988. Pose and combined gestures have the highest point estimates, whereas expressions show no clear improvement. Hand occlusion against FaceFusion, configured with an occlusion mask, scores below the static baseline. The end-to-end time required to satisfy the validator also distinguishes attacks from genuine sessions, achieving a session-level AUC of 0.732, although this signal includes synthesis and transport delays. These results show that challenge sets should be tested against current attack configurations and that response time can provide an additional, deployment-specific signal.

title: Minimal Subsystems for Characterizing Genuine Multipartite Entanglement
abstract: Genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) is a valuable resource for quantum technologies, but quantifying it in many-body systems can be demanding since measures defined through optimizations over bipartitions are often assumed to require large joint measurements and many measurement settings. We introduce the concepts of GME evaluation length and GME evaluation number, which capture, respectively, the largest subsystem that must be jointly measured and the number of distinct subsystems that need to be measured to evaluate multipartite entanglement measures defined via bipartition optimizations. Taking the genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC) as a canonical example, we show that, for $N$-qubit Haar-random pure states, the GMC can be evaluated using only $N$ single-qubit purity measurements. Thus, for typical many-body states, evaluating the GMC requires considering only the $N$ single-site bipartitions, rather than the exponentially many distinct bipartitions. We further corroborate this behavior numerically for physically accessible states generated by local random quantum circuits. Our results show that the practical cost of quantifying GME can be dramatically lower than suggested by its formal definition, establishing measurement complexity as a complementary operational lens for multipartite entanglement.

title: Unravel: Recovering an Interactive 3D Scene from a Single Image
abstract: We present Unravel, a training-free framework that turns a single image into an interactive 3D scene, where every object is an independent and movable asset. Existing generators either produce one entangled geometry in which no object can be moved, or predict all objects in one feed-forward pass, where a wrong guess cannot be detected or repaired. Unravel instead takes a different approach: it first takes the scene apart, and then puts it back together. Starting from the input image, an agentic harness that iteratively peels the image layer by layer, and adopts point cloud as major modality for spatial relationship recovery. Specifically, a vision-language model plans which objects are fully visible, an image editor removes them and restores the occluded regions. Every edit is verified before being incorporated into the reconstruction. This process gradually turns occluded parts of the scene into direct observation, allowing objects to be reconstructed when they are best exposed rather than hallucinated from the original image alone. The scene is then rebuilt in reverse removal order, so that the supporting objects are naturally placed before the objects they support. Since a single-view image only reveals part of an object, we treat the observed points as a lower bound on its size: an asset may grow to cover its points, but can not shrink away from them. Finally, we physically settle the reconstructed scene to remove floating objects and interpenetrations, followed by an agentic audit that corrects remaining placement errors. Extensive experiments on diverse indoor scenes show that Unravel recovers more objects, places them more faithfully, and produces scenes that are more physically-plausible than existing methods.

title: What Can We Learn About an AI We Cannot Access?: Reverse-Engineering Evidence from OpenAI’s 2026 Mathematics Corpus and the Limits of Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Research OverviewWhat can we learn about an artificial intelligence system when we can observe its scientific discoveries but cannot access the model itself?In October 2026, OpenAI publicly released a substantial collection of mathematical research generated using an unreleased frontier AI model. While these publications reveal mathematical results, proofs, and selected reasoning summaries, the underlying neural mechanisms remain inaccessible.This study investigates the scientific possibilities and limitations of reverse-engineering mathematical reasoning from such public artifacts, bridging black-box AI interpretability, mathematical reasoning, reproducible computational research, and mechanistic interpretability.Using a pinned version of OpenAI's 2026 Mathematics Corpus, we conduct a reproducible structural audit covering 719 mathematical manuscripts across 372 result families, including 242 families with Lean scope documents and 10 publicly released abridged reasoning summaries.An expanded analysis inventories 133,955 versioned Git objects (2.06 GiB), including 122,876 Lean source files and 8,007 preprint TeX source files. This establishes a traceable structural record of the public release without claiming to have semantically verified every mathematical result.To investigate the distinction between observable reasoning and internal computation, we separately conduct causal residual-stream activation-patching experiments using four independently initialized, fully inspectable toy Transformers. These experiments demonstrate how internal computational effects can be tested through controlled interventions, while explicitly distinguishing the findings from the inaccessible OpenAI model.Scientific ContributionsThe study provides a reproducible inventory of OpenAI's public mathematical research artifacts, an empirical examination of their organization, a controlled demonstration of causal intervention methodology, and an evidence-based account of what public mathematical outputs can and cannot reveal about an unreleased AI system.Rather than claiming to have recovered proprietary model internals, the research establishes a methodological foundation for future investigations connecting mathematical proof structures, observable reasoning behavior, and causal mechanisms in accessible AI models.Open Science and ReproducibilityThe accompanying open-source repository provides research code, experimental protocols, provenance records, derived datasets, figures, statistical analyses, and reproducibility documentation.Research repository: https://github.com/taechasith/What-2026OpenAI-HidesAuthor: Taechasith KangkhuntodAffiliations:School of Engineering, University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, ThailandCoeus Technology, CreativeLabTH GroupKeywords: Mechanistic Interpretability; Black-Box AI Interpretability; Mathematical Reasoning; AI-Generated Mathematics; Reverse Engineering; Causal Intervention; Reproducible Research

title: Advanced Reasoning of Quality Valued Configurations in Category Theory
abstract: # Advanced Reasoning of Quality Valued Configurations in Category Theory This repository contains the replication package (models, operations, and empirical results) for the paper **"Advanced Reasoning of Quality Valued Configurations in Category Theory"**, currently **UNDER REVIEW** at *ELSEVIER Array* journal. This dataset serves as supplementary material to support the reproducibility of the experiments and case studies presented in the manuscript. ## 📂 Repository Structure The repository is organized as follows: * **/Models**: Contains the 4 full (folders `a`) and 4 sampled (folders `b`) feature-wise quality-measured SPLs. Each model is provided in 3 formats to support different solvers: * `.cql`: For **QVM/CQL IDE** (Our approach). Includes the code for the 6 quality-aware reasoning operations: `SATISFY`, `COUNT`, `FILTER`, `BOUND`, `RANDOM`, and `AGGREGATE`. * `.uvl`: For **UVLS/Z3**. * `.txt` / `.js`: For **HADAS/Clafer**.* **/QAsCSVs**: Contains the variant-wise Quality Attributes (QAs) data: * `a)` 4 Large CSVs corresponding to the **complete** solution space. * `b)` 4 CSVs corresponding to the **randomly sampled** solution space.* **ElsevierARRAY_EvaluationResults&Statistics.xlsx**: A Microsoft Excel file containing the raw scalability results, performance comparison, and statistical analyses for non-linear regression approximation functions. ## 🛠️ Automated Reasoners & Tools This repository focuses on the data and models. The automated reasoners used for the evaluation are third-party tools available at their official repositories: * **CQL IDE** (Required for `.cql` files): [https://github.com/CategoricalData/CQL](https://github.com/CategoricalData/CQL)* **UVLS**: [https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=caradhras.uvls-code](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=caradhras.uvls-code)* **HADAS**: [https://hadas.caosd.lcc.uma.es/](https://hadas.caosd.lcc.uma.es/) ## 🚀 Usage & Requirements The dataset generation and experiments were conducted using **Java JDK 17.0.11**. To replicate the QVM experiments:1. Download and install the **CQL IDE** from the link above.2. Open the desired `.cql` file from the `/Models` directory.3. Execute the operations defined within the file (SATISFY, FILTER, etc.) to observe the output. ### Synthetic QA valuesThe SPL models are taken from the literature, but their QA values are synthetic, because no comparable fully measured SPLs are available. Each QA value was drawn independently and uniformly at random, as an integer within a fixed range per QA, or as a Boolean with equal probability:**Variant-wise:**- EDGE: `Time` and `Energy` in [1, 1000].- Trimesh and MobileMedia: `Cache` in [1, 8000] and a fixed `Cost` of 100.- WeaFQAs: `Dependencies` in [1, 10] and a Boolean `Tested`.**Feature-wise:**- EDGE: `Cost` up to 25 and `Security` in {L, M, H}.- Trimesh and MobileMedia: `CodeLines` up to 100,000.- WeaFQAs: `Usability` in [1, 10] and a Boolean `Cloud`. The sampled files in `QAsCSVs/bSampling` were drawn independently of the complete files in `QAsCSVs/aFull`. The generation seeds were not kept, so the published CSV and model files are the reference data, and every tool was run on these same files. For HADAS/Clafer only, feature-wise values were rescaled to [-10, 10] so that their aggregation stays within Clafer's Integer domain. ## 📄 License This project is licensed under the **MIT License** - see the LICENSE file for details.

title: Data and code for: Who wins depends on who judges: re-grading published LoCoMo and LongMemEval answers of agent memory systems
abstract: Verdicts, labels, tables and code for a study of how published long-term memory leaderboards for LLM agents depend on the LLM judge. The 47,253 unique answers that vendors and third parties published for 50 answer sets (36 LoCoMo, 14 LongMemEval-S; 10 memory products and 9 baselines) were re-graded by a grid of 20 judge configurations (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-5-mini on both benchmarks, gpt-4o on LongMemEval-S only, each with five prompts): 737,115 verdicts. A reference judge (gpt-5.4, reasoning effort low) graded 5,000 of the answers under the same five prompts: 25,000 verdicts. 250 disputed answers carry three-way labels (CORRECT, PARTIAL, WRONG) from an LLM annotator in two independent blind passes; these are model labels, not human labels. Question, gold and answer texts and raw judge replies are not included, because they belong to the benchmark authors and the vendors or can quote them. Every key resolves to the public source files listed with URL, commit and SHA-256 in code/manifest.json, and the included code rebuilds the aligned answers. See README.md.

title: Applying automatic speaker recognition systems to cross-language forensic voice comparison
abstract: Abstract Forensic voice comparison (FVC) is usually conducted to assist legal systems in forming a view of whether the recordings of a nominal suspect and those of a nominal offender are from the same individual or not. In the past decade, forensic practitioners have increasingly used automatic speaker recognition (ASR) systems, a form of AI technology, in their FVC. This paper illustrates how AI technologies impact the research and practice of FVC by reviewing the methods and approaches in FVC in the present and the past. A study of cross-language FVC is presented to showcase how ASR systems are used to tackle difficult tasks in FVC: 21 female and 22 male Cantonese–English–Mandarin trilingual speakers are tested in both language-matched and language-mismatch conditions using an x-vector ASR system. Results show that the performance of the ASR system is outstanding even when the nominal suspect and nominal offender spoke different languages (i.e., language-mismatch conditions). The paper also discusses the general impact of AI technology on forensic phonetics and brings new insights to forensic linguistics.
