title: Language creation in multi-agent systems
abstract: Το αντικείμενο μελέτης της παρούσας διπλωματικής εργασίας είναι τα συστήματα δύο πρακτόρων οι οποίοι εκπαιδεύονται και συνεργάζονται, ανταλλάσσοντας πληροφορίες, με στόχο την επίτευξη ενός κοινού στόχου. Για την επίτευξη αυτού του στόχου, οι πράκτορες μπορούν να αναπτύξουν μια δική τους γλώσσα “ab initio” ή να εξελίξουν μια ήδη υπάρχουσα. Το συγκεκριμένο θέμα είναι αρκετά πολύπλοκο και γι’ αυτό απαιτείται λεπτομερής ανάλυση της θεωρίας πίσω από αυτό. Αρχικά, γίνεται μια περιγραφή της επεξεργασίας φυσικής γλώσσας και των τομέων από τους οποίους αυτή αποτελείται.Έπειτα γίνεται εισαγωγή στις έννοιες της μηχανικής εκμάθησης, της βαθιάς μάθησης και της ενισχυτικής μάθησης, με ιδιαίτερη έμφαση στην αρχιτεκτονική των μοντέλων και αλγορίθμων που χρησιμοποιούνται στην εκπαίδευση των πολυπρακτορικών συστημάτων. Στη συνέχεια γίνεται παρουσίαση ενός εκ των πειραμάτων που διαπραγματεύονται το θέμα. Συγκεκριμένα, αναλύεται η έρευνα που πραγματοποιήθηκε στο τμήμα Έρευνας Τεχνητής Νοημοσύνης της εταιρείας Facebook με τίτλο “Deal or No Deal? End-to-End Learning for Negotiation Dialogues”, με στόχο να διερευνηθεί πώς δύο πράκτορες, που λειτουργούν σε ένα παιχνίδι διαπραγμάτευσης, μπορούν να δημιουργήσουν ή να βελτιώσουν από κοινού μια γλώσσα για επίτευξη επιτυχημένων αποτελεσμάτων. Η μελέτη αντλεί έμπνευση από διαπραγματεύσεις μεταξύ ανθρώπων σε μια διαπραγματευτική εργασία, όπου οι πράκτορες δεν έχουν άμεση πρόσβαση ο ένας στη συνάρτηση ανταμοιβής του άλλου και πρέπει να βασίζονται στον διάλογο με φυσική γλώσσα για να αυξήσουν το προσωπικό τους σκορ έναντι του αντιπάλου, συμφωνώντας στην τελική ανταλλαγή αντικειμένων που για τον καθένα έχει διαφορετική αξία. Με βάση αυτά τα στοιχεία, η διατριβή εισάγει τα Μεγάλα Γλωσσικά Μοντέλα (LLM) ως εναλλακτική προσέγγιση για το ίδιο διαπραγματευτικό έργο, με αφορμή τη γλωσσική ικανότητα που επιδεικνύουν πλέον τα μοντέλα αυτά. Για το λόγο αυτό, σχεδιάζονται και αξιολογούνται τρεις πειραματικές συνθήκες στο ίδιο διαπραγματευτικό παιχνίδι. Στην πρώτη, οι πράκτορες LLM διαπραγματεύονται χωρίς προηγούμενη εκπαίδευση ή ανατροφοδότηση, προκειμένου να διαπιστωθεί πώς συγκρίνονται με τους αρχικούς πράκτορες που έχουν εκπαιδευτεί ειδικά για τη συγκεκριμένη εργασία. Στη δεύτερη, σε έναν πράκτορα παρέχονται τα δικά του προηγούμενα πρακτικά διαπραγματεύσεων και αποτελέσματα ως πλαίσιο μεταξύ των γύρων, χωρίς καμία αλλαγή στις παραμέτρους του μοντέλου, προκειμένου να ελεγχθεί εάν η εμπειρία από μόνη της μπορεί να βελτιώσει την απόδοση. Στην τρίτη, ένα ξεχωριστό μοντέλο λειτουργεί ως κριτικός, εξετάζοντας τις διαπραγματεύσεις ενός πράκτορα και παρέχοντας στοχευμένες προτάσεις βελτίωσης μεταξύ των γύρων. Συνολικά, αυτά τα πειράματα συγκρίνουν την ικανότητα διαπραγμάτευσης των σύγχρονων γλωσσικών μοντέλων, τόσο των μη εκπαιδευμένων όσο και εκείνων που έχουν βελτιωθεί αποκλειστικά μέσω του πλαισίου, με το αρχικό σύστημα που έχει εκπαιδευτεί από άκρο σε άκρο.

title: Nyāya-Pramāṇa: A Neuro-Symbolic Epistemic Verification Framework for Calibrated, Provenance-Aware LLM Reasoning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional generative fluency but suffer from critical epistemic vulnerabilities: severe overconfidence on ungrounded propositions, inability to differentiate direct empirical observation from unverified textual hearsay (modality flattening), susceptibility to sycophantic hallucinations, and lack of mechanisms to invalidate obsolete beliefs. While retrieval-augmented generation and tool-use frameworks mitigate some factual errors, they lack a principled epistemic hierarchy to constrain subjective beliefs or invalidate flawed deductive steps. In this paper, we introduce Nyāya-Pramāṇa, a neuro-symbolic epistemic verification framework rooted in classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika epistemology. Nyāya-Pramāṇa enforces a dual-system cognitive architecture: an unconstrained System 1 LLM proposer (Manas) generates structured 5-part deductive arguments (Pañcāvayava), which are audited by a deterministic System 2 epistemic verifier (Buddhi). The verifier enforces a six-tier evidence modality hierarchy (Pramāṇa), applies empirical confidence ceilings, intercepts seven cognitive fallacies (Adhyāsa), validates causal claims via interventional do-calculus simulations, and updates a semantic vector belief store (Citta) equipped with automated truth sublation (Bādha). Across empirical evaluations, our framework demonstrates:1. Calibrated Confidence: Achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.0670 and a Brier Score of 0.1727, outperforming standard uncalibrated LLM overconfidence (ECE > 0.25);2. Fallacy Interception: Intercepts 100.0% of adversarial queries across 50 benchmark cases spanning correlation-causation confusion, scope inflation, sycophancy, and hearsay misattribution;3. Calibrated Abstention on TruthfulQA: Correctly abstains on 40.0% of ungrounded or subjective queries with machine-readable codes, while verifying ground-truth scientific claims with zero conversational hallucination.

title: Is forgetting in post-trained language models just a shift in vocabulary bias?
abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final word predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a single confidence dial (temperature). Adjusting the vocabulary bias fixes very little: under 10% of the loss increase. Combining it with a temperature recovers up to 36%, and the models where it helps most are clearly overconfident on this text. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the same bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the loss increase stays out of reach of these context-free corrections. Code and per-document data: 10.5281/zenodo.23304208. Use of AI tools The author chose the question and the models, and checked the results. AI coding and writing assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini, ChatGPT) were used to help write and run the code, make the figures and tables, and edit and fact-check the text. The author is responsible for the content.

abstract: Επιλεγμένα αποσπάσματα από το βιβλίο «ΕΠΙΣΤΗΜΟΛΟΓΙΑ ΤΗΣ ΛΟΓΙΚΗΣΛογική – Διαλεκτική ή Θεωρία της Γνώσης» του Επαμεινώνδα Ξενόπουλου, σχετικά με την επιστημολογία της λογικής. title: pyweatherfiles
abstract: pyweatherfiles 0.0.1 First public release of pyweatherfiles, a toolkit for Typical Meteorological Year (TMY) generation and weather-data workflows. Highlights Published the source distribution and universal wheel to PyPI. Declares support for Python 3.10 through 3.13. Includes the full documentation on Read the Docs and its self-contained Seville-Madrid case-study tutorial. Validation twine check passed for the wheel and source distribution. Both artifacts and the TestPyPI publication were installed in clean virtual environments; package metadata/runtime versions and pip check passed. Release validation completed with 424 passing tests and 11 skips for unavailable optional IDF fixtures. Scope The external climate-data acquisition module remains outside the scope of this first release.

title: State-preparation costs in exact conjunction learning
abstract: Exact learning of a positive conjunction requires states in which membership queries can be evaluated. We study the cost of preparing these states for an unknown set of at most $d$ prerequisites among $n$ independent providers. Each provider operation costs one unit, and each nonmutating query costs $c$. If every query state is rebuilt from empty, the deterministic minimax cost is $\Theta(nd+cd\log_2(1+n/d))$. If one current state can be retained and individual providers can be activated or removed, the cost is $\Theta(n+cd\log_2(1+n/d))$. Both interfaces allow free whole-state disposal. A failure-path certificate proves the rebuilding lower bound, while breadth-first elimination and reversible block splitting simultaneously attain the appropriate preparation and query bounds. We also determine exact costs when all subsets are admissible. The resulting cost ratio characterizes when state reuse yields an improvement of order $d$. Finite enumeration checks the constructions and exhibits instances where elementary elimination has better constants. Preprint; not peer reviewed. Replication materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23298237

title: MoE-Based Anomaly Detection of High-Altitude UAV Flight Data
abstract: Analyzing flight data from high-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is an essential approach to anomaly detection and early warning. However, flight data collected during the climb, cruise, and descent phases of high-altitude UAV missions exhibit pronounced distributional differences, making it difficult for existing anomaly detection methods to establish a unified model of normal flight behavior across all phases, thereby constraining detection accuracy. To address this, this paper proposes an anomaly detection method for high-altitude UAV flight data based on a Mixture of Experts (MoE). Specifically, a Multi-Scale Dual-Path Mixture-of-Experts encoder is constructed to extract local perturbations from UAV flight sequences; multi-scale convolution, a Transformer, and a dual-path LSTM are fused to capture temporal dependencies within the flight data; and a gating network automatically adapts to and uniformly models the data distributions across different mission phases. Furthermore, a two-stage reconstruction error is employed to construct sliding-window anomaly scores, and the median absolute deviation (MAD) is adopted to adaptively determine the anomaly decision threshold, enabling detection of flight-data anomalies across all mission phases. Experimental results on a self-constructed high-altitude UAV flight dataset with controlled anomaly injections demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a window F1 of 93.97% and an event recall of 91.77% across three independent training seeds.

title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .

title: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.

title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation
abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.

title: NANO: A Unified Optimization Framework for Nonlinear Gaussian Filtering
abstract: Conventional Gaussian filtering typically approximates nonlinear models or their statistical moments and retains the Kalman update structure. The resulting approximation errors can affect both state estimates and their uncertainty. This paper presents the Natural Gradient Gaussian Approximation (NANO) framework for nonlinear filtering. Both prediction and measurement update are formulated as optimization problems over Gaussian distributions, with the entire Gaussian distribution serving as the optimization variable. The framework integrates observation losses, distributional discrepancies, natural-gradient optimization, and finite-step update rules, providing a unified formulation for constructing different filters. Natural-gradient iterations account for the geometry of the Gaussian family and jointly update the distribution parameters. The framework incorporates the existing NANO-P method using the Kullback-Leibler divergence and introduces NANO-W using the Wasserstein distance. NANO-P maintains covariance positive definiteness through a positive-semidefinite curvature approximation, while NANO-W uses a covariance transport update that accommodates indefinite curvature. Their update rules and sufficient conditions for covariance positive definiteness are established within the common framework. Through these two realizations, the proposed framework achieves the best estimation accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of six benchmarks. Runtime evaluations further assess its computational feasibility for practical applications.

title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
abstract: Guided sampling with sparse observations and PDE residuals has recently been combined with neural operator priors to solve partial differential equations in function space, their natural setting. We pair such a prior with pseudo-bootstrap sequential Monte Carlo (pBS SMC), a guided sampling framework that accommodates proposals without tractable densities, and introduce a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting. Across five benchmark PDE systems this proposal attains the best error--time trade-off at every step count tested, and wrapping it in pBS gives the lowest error on most inverse-problem settings, with the largest gains when few sampling steps are used.

title: Flux-tunable transmon with an Al/AlOx/4Hb-TaS2 Josephson junction
abstract: Incorporating van der Waals (vdW) superconductors into Josephson elements extends circuit-QED beyond conventional Al/AlOx/Al junctions, enabling microwave probes of unconventional condensates and subgap excitations.We realize a flux-tunable transmon whose nonlinear inductive element is an Al/AlOx/4Hb-TaS2 Josephson junction, with a tunnel barrier form by full in-situ oxidation of ultrathin Al layers on an exfoliated 4Hb-TaS2 flake in a process compatible with standard transmon fabrication.In a three-dimensional copper cavity, the device shows a SQUID-like flux-dependent spectrum that is well reproduced by a dressed transmon--cavity Hamiltonian in the transmon regime.We measure sub-microsecond energy relaxation (T1 = 0.08--0.69 μs), while Ramsey measurements indicate dephasing faster than our 16 ns resolution.A naive Ambegaokar--Baratoff comparison using room-temperature junction resistances gives a suppressed effective energy scale; however, cross-sectional TEM reveals an amorphous region at the TaS2 interface, most likely produced by the pre-deposition ion-milling step.We therefore attribute the suppressed EJRn product primarily to a non-ideal hybrid interface.This work demonstrates the integration of 4Hb-TaS2 into a circuit-QED device and establishes an interface-optimization baseline for future edge-sensitive designs targeting boundary and subgap degrees of freedom in vdW superconductors.

title: What is artificial intelligence used for in food production lines? A task by method cross-tabulation of a Scopus corpus. Supplementary material: code, result files and figures
abstract: Supplementary material for the article "What is artificial intelligence used for in food production lines? A task by method cross-tabulation of a Scopus corpus". The deposit contains the analysis code, every result file the code writes, the execution log and the fifteen figures of the article. Corpus: a single Scopus extraction of 866 records queried on title, abstract and keywords, reduced to 862 documents published between 1975 and 2026, on artificial intelligence applied to food production lines. The Scopus export itself is not redistributed here, because the Scopus licence does not permit the public redistribution of a substantial portion of the database. The full search equation, the field queried and the extraction date are printed at the top of the execution log, so that the export can be reconstructed by any reader with Scopus access. Contents: pipeline_EN.py, the analysis script; figures_EN.py, which writes the fifteen figures; comparaison_consolidation_tableauA.py, which measures the effect of reference-variant consolidation; eighteen result files in CSV; the execution log; the fifteen figures in PNG at 300 dpi; and a checksum file listing the MD5 digest of every item. The README describes the reproduction procedure, the fixed parameters and their line numbers. The pipeline is deterministic. A cold run in an empty directory reproduces every figure reported in the article.

title: SELF-HEALING QUANTUM SENSOR INFRASTRUCTURE AND RECONFIGURABLE MATTER AT THE LIMIT Module Replacement × Calibration Recovery × Service Continuity This exploratory engineering monograph develops a falsifiable research architecture for modular quantum-enabled and classical sensor infrastructure that must continue providing scientifically valid measurements despite component failure, material aging, vendor discontinuity, shared-reference faults and partial loss of maintenance capability. The central question is not whether a network can switch its modules or restart operation. It is whether that network can recover a traceable measurand, independently verify accepted functions, constrain autonomous repair authority and maintain a reliable fallback or retirement path when restoration is impossible or unsafe. The synthesis combines three prior mother architectures while distinguishing inherited methods from unverified integration hypotheses. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, especially chapters 52–64, contributes modular reconfiguration, robot maintenance, repairability, physical interfaces and quality assurance. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 41–49 and 75–82, contributes fault isolation, graded authority, service recovery, classical fallback and reconstructible handoffs. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, especially chapters 49–64, contributes reference integrity, package drift, calibration recovery, common-mode failure detection and replacement continuity. Those original works are methodological sources, not experimental demonstrations of a finished self-healing quantum–nano infrastructure. The proposed core relation is R_post = (F_verified_after/F_required) × P_trace × P_recover. It is a normalized design heuristic rather than a universal physical law or safety certificate. F_verified_after represents the independently confirmed functions following repair; F_required is the explicitly declared essential service scope. P_trace and P_recover describe traceability and verified recovery, respectively. Their possible statistical dependence, calibration uncertainty, hidden physical wear and categorical scientific or safety vetoes must be evaluated separately. A powered-on replacement cannot count as a successful repair when the old measurand cannot be reconstructed, independent calibration is missing or the new connector causes hidden drift. The research program defines the Replace–Recalibrate–Verify–Rollback protocol. Each event preserves the old reference state, instrument serial number, raw observations, material and connector information, authority, operator identity, calibration uncertainty and independent acceptance results. Two coupled maps—physical module topology and calibration-reference dependency graph—make visible how a local intervention can change network measurement interpretation. The project permits repair, partial restoration, classical fallback, safe service reduction, full replacement and responsible retirement as legitimate possible outcomes. The monograph comprises 82 chapters with 12 separately paginated research units per chapter, 30 concise physics and mathematical derivation plates, one candidate chapter relation and spatial reconfiguration model per chapter, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Every Gate and Embryo is linked to one of 233 numbered equation eggs that draw on recognized relations in probability, mechanics, statistical uncertainty, control and reliability; the equation eggs are not new physical laws. Chapters use a common comparative research grammar, so programmatically counted words should not be confused with an equal quantity of independent scientific discoveries or fully proved theorems. Proposed experiments compare qualified manual replacement, centralized maintenance, fixed spare-node redundancy and distributed robotic repair with a matched classical-only sensing baseline. A module network is challenged through connector damage, alignment drift, thermal fatigue, forged component identity, expired reference artifacts, firmware regressions, power loss and common-mode calibration failure. Blinded replacement batches and independent laboratory replays evaluate scientific recovery and lifecycle burden rather than merely counting restored packets or achieving low machine-learning loss. The Research Gates workbook provides chapter and page navigation, 200 falsifiable studies, 33 provisional Answer Embryos, physics-plate and equation-egg indices, a module replacement register, calibration lineage, fault injection matrix, recovery closeout, human authority, lifecycle economics and three-source continuity. It is intended as an extendable research apparatus for successor investigators, not as evidence that the listed experiments have been performed. SCIENTIFIC AND DEPLOYMENT BOUNDARIES. No claim is made that quantum sensing is always superior to qualified classical alter

title: A Temporal-Error State Architecture for Long-Horizon AI Agents
abstract: This record contains a research architecture proposal and evaluation protocol for the Temporal-Episodic Agent Architecture (TEAA), focused on long-horizon AI agents that must reason under deadlines, estimate task completion time, and adapt after execution failures. The proposed architecture introduces a candidate Continuous Temporal-Error State (CTES) module intended to represent elapsed time, remaining deadline, estimated task progress, predicted completion time, and prediction error. A separate episodic memory store preserves timestamped events and outcomes, while a retrieval controller selects relevant past experiences for use by a large language model (LLM)-based agent. The manuscript defines research questions, candidate mathematical formulations, baseline systems, ablation studies, evaluation metrics, and safety considerations. Its central hypothesis is that a trainable temporal-error state may improve deadline-sensitive task performance compared with prompt-based time injection and simpler recurrent-state baselines under matched computational budgets. Research status: This is a research proposal and evaluation protocol. It does not report completed experiments or validated performance improvements. The novelty and practical benefits of the proposed mechanism remain to be established through implementation, systematic comparison with prior work, and reproducible experiments.

title: Rapid Epicentral Distance and Magnitude Estimation via Collaborative Attention Network
abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid and reliable estimation of epicentral distance and magnitude are pivotal for damage assessment in earthquake early warning (EEW). However, conventional epicentral distance and magnitude estimation approaches for EEW rely primarily on manually defined features to construct empirical prediction equations. Meanwhile, many existing machine learning models focus solely on single tasks (either epicentral distance or magnitude estimation alone), neglecting the correlation and impact between epicentral distance and magnitude. In this study, we design a collaborative attention network (CAN) framework for EEW, named EEWCAN, which combines global and local attention mechanisms. In addition, we explore the feasibility of EEWCAN for estimating epicentral distance and magnitude from single-station data in the Japan region. EEWCAN integrates global and local attention mechanisms to automatically capture more critical features pertinent to epicentral distance and magnitude from seismic waveforms. The EEWCAN framework is composed of two models: the EEWCAN-Dis model for epicentral distance estimation and the EEWCAN-Mag model for magnitude estimation. Meanwhile, the epicentral distance estimated by the EEWCAN-Dis model is incorporated into the EEWCAN-Mag model. We trained and tested EEWCAN using seismic events recorded by the Kyoshin network in Japan, with waveforms serving as the input to EEWCAN. The test results demonstrate that, when data from 3 s after P-wave onset are used, EEWCAN can obtain reliable estimates of epicentral distance and magnitude, outperforming the baseline models. Furthermore, by incorporating the estimated epicentral distance information, EEWCAN enhances the reliability of magnitude estimation. This result demonstrates that our proposed method can provide a certain degree of reliability for epicentral distance and magnitude estimation in EEW.

title: Fixed-qubit CVaR-VQE and quantum-inspired QUBO sampling for static and dynamic restricted vertex multicut in telecom resilience
abstract: A central question in hybrid quantum–classical optimization is how to assign the classical and quantum components according to the structure of the problem, rather than attempting to transfer the full optimization model to a quantum device. We investigate this question on static and finite-horizon dynamic restricted vertex minimum multicut, an NP-hard network-isolation problem with exponentially many path constraints. A classical row-generation layer handles graph separation, feasibility verification, and constraint generation, while quantum or quantum-inspired samplers are used only for the current restricted optimization problem. We develop two such algorithms: an exact-slack QUBO formulation sampled by simulated annealing, and a fixed-register CVaR-VQE formulation in which generated constraints modify a classical loss without enlarging the static quantum register. Exact MILP row generation provides the certifying reference. Experiments on SNDlib-derived telecom instances show that both approaches can be integrated consistently within this workflow, while classical-sampler controls do not establish a quantum-specific performance advantage. The dynamic study further shows how temporal coupling creates a distinct resource bottleneck, motivating decomposed formulations for larger horizons.

title: Nonlinear delay-embedded photonic reservoir computing for multi-step ahead prediction
abstract: Photonic reservoir computing exploits the nonlinear mapping capability of optical systems to enable efficient time-series processing, offering high speed, large bandwidth, and low power consumption. However, existing studies mainly focus on one-step prediction, while multi-step ahead prediction for nonlinear dynamical systems remains challenging. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a nonlinear delay-embedded photonic reservoir computing (NDE-PRC), in which nonlinear combinations of delayed inputs are introduced to enhance multi-step ahead prediction. The resulting interwoven dynamics enrich the reservoir’s nonlinear complexity and memory capacity, enabling accurate multi-step prediction up to 20-steps with accelerated processing speed. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits improved robustness to system parameters, achieving reliable multi-step prediction over a significantly expanded parameter regime. Overall, our results demonstrate an effective and scalable approach for accurate and robust multi-step prediction of nonlinear dynamical systems, highlighting the potential of photonic reservoir computing for advanced temporal information processing.

title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. evidence.title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
evidence.abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. title: AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version
abstract: Accurate long-term air quality forecasting is challenging due to long-range transport, meteorological variability, and nonlinear chemical reactions underlying secondary pollutant formation. Purely data-driven models often suffer from long-horizon drift and lack physical consistency, while existing physics-informed approaches commonly follow open-loop designs that fuse neural and physical components only at the output level. We propose AeroChem, a closed-loop physics-informed state space framework for chemically reactive air quality forecasting. AeroChem adopts a two-branch co-correction design: a UDE-based process branch provides a structured but imperfect physical prior, while a Mamba-based virtual measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and produces probabilistic virtual observations. Neural Kalman Fusion couples the two branches by correcting the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeding the posterior state back into the simulator, reducing long-horizon drift. We further introduce HanoiAir, a real-world dataset integrating pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories. Experiments on HanoiAir and a public benchmark show that AeroChem improves long-horizon stability and sudden-change forecasting.

title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

title: ProMoDD: Dataset Distillation for 3D Human Motion via Prototype-Conditioned Diffusion Models
abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to retain the training utility of a large dataset in a much smaller set of examples. For skeleton-based action recognition, this requires capturing discriminative motion variation without disrupting the geometry and temporal continuity of articulated bodies. Directly optimizing joint coordinates can violate these constraints, while plausible motion generation alone does not ensure useful training examples. We propose Prototype-Conditioned Motion Dataset Distillation (ProMoDD), which conditions a motion diffusion model on class-wise prototypes of temporally resolved recognition features. We further tailor diffusion training to motion data, enabling the generator to model both skeletal configurations and their temporal evolution. We then construct each compact training set through budget-aware hybrid selection: representative real sequences cover densely populated regions of the pooled recognition space, while selected generated candidates complement them in less-populated regions. This couples prototype-guided generation with feature-space selection, balancing the reliability of observed motions with the variation of synthesis under a fixed per-class sequence budget. Across five difficulty-stratified subsets of the single-person classes in NTU RGB+D 60, ProMoDD achieves its largest gains under tight distillation budgets, reaching 40.32% top-1 accuracy on Full49 with three sequences per class, 4.57 percentage points above class-wise k-means. These gains reflect the complete framework. The same distilled sets train ST-GCN, MS-G3D, and CTR-GCN without regeneration.

title: QIAP: A Quantum-Inspired Authentication Protocol with BB84-Based Channel Monitoring
abstract: Authentication in quantum-aware communication settings requires mechanisms that verify user legitimacy while also assessing whether the communication channel exhibits excessive disturbance. This paper presents QIAP, a stateful hybrid framework that combines classical commitment-based challenge-response authentication with BB84-based quantum-channel monitoring. QIAP uses a dual-branch verification structure inspired by rectilinear and diagonal basis selection. In the rectilinear branch, the prover opens a hash-based commitment and the verifier checks consistency with the registered round token. In the diagonal branch, the prover returns an HMAC tag bound to the verifier nonce, round identifier, and submitted commitment without disclosing the round-specific sub-secret. Under the stated hash, HMAC, freshness, secure-registration, protected-storage, and high-entropy-secret assumptions, QIAP provides computational resistance to the modeled wrong-secret and replay attempts and protects the long-term master secret from direct recovery. After successful authentication, the BB84 module estimates the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and aborts the session when the measured value reaches or exceeds the configured threshold. In the reported simulation, no successful authentication was observed among 1,000 tested wrong-secret attempts per branch. The baseline and full intercept-resend conditions produced mean QBER values of approximately 0.02 and 0.25, respectively. The classical authentication stage required approximately 0.6 ms, and the implemented authentication messages required approximately 113 bytes per round. These results indicate that QIAP can provide a lightweight hybrid framework for combining secret-based identity verification with QBER-based channel-disturbance assessment under the stated threat model.

title: Beyond Quantization: Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning via Masked Hilbert Envelope Prediction
abstract: Current self-supervised speech models typically avoid predicting raw time-domain waveforms directly because fast phase shifts cause instability. To bypass this, popular methods use vector-quantized codebooks, multi-stage clustering, or teacher networks, but these approaches can suffer from memory bloat, complex pipelines, and codebook collapse. This study introduces Masked Hilbert Envelope Prediction (MHEP), a streamlined, non-quantized pre-training approach that treats masked speech modeling as a continuous regression task based on instantaneous analytic envelopes. By filtering clean speech through a frozen Constant-Q Gabor filterbank, MHEP separates vocal-tract modulation from the carrier phase, generating a stable, phase-invariant target without relying on codebooks or auxiliary teacher models. In downstream speaker verification tasks, while standard waveform regression and STFT spectrogram reconstruction cause performance drops (10.60% and 9.80% Equal Error Rates, respectively) compared to a random baseline (8.00% EER), MHEP avoids this negative transfer and improves performance to 7.40% EER. When scaled to 100 hours of LibriSpeech data, MHEP pre-training prevents optimization failure in deep 8-layer Transformers and drastically reduces the downstream verification error from 34.90% to 10.90% EER, achieving a 68.8% relative error reduction.

title: A Fast Quantitative Analyzer for NetKAT (Artifact)
abstract: Artifact: A Fast Quantitative Analyzer for NetKAT (POPL’27) This artifact contains every tool from the paper’s evaluation in one Docker image (prebuilt for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64), the input data for every experiment, and the original results behind the paper’s figures and claims. wspp-artifact/ README.md this file experiments/ one script per class of experiment (see below) results/ output of the experiment scripts (created on first run) figures/ output of experiments/plot.sh (created on first run) run.sh run any tool in the container, with data/ mounted at /data smoke.sh run every engine once on small inputs (a few minutes) images/ prebuilt Docker images (+ .sha256) data/ experiment inputs; see data/README.md original-results/ our recorded results; see original-results/README.md docker/ the tools' source code (docker/src/) and everything needed to rebuild the images Getting started Requirements: Docker. Images: about 1 GB compressed, 5 GB loaded. docker load -i images/wspp-artifact-amd64.tar.gz # or -arm64 on Apple Silicon / ARM ./run.sh artifact-tools # tool catalogue, versions, source provenance ./smoke.sh # expect: smoke: 24 passed, 0 failed run.sh picks the image matching the host architecture (--arch amd64|arm64 overrides) and mounts data/ read-only at /data, so inputs are named /data/ . OUT_DIR= additionally mounts a writable /out. Tools Tool (paper name) Commands in the image Source Neko (our tool) neko, ablation builds neko-ablate-*, neko-noopt docker/src/neko (Rust) Neko case-study tooling neko-benchmark-cdf, neko-trace-bench docker/src/neko-networks Lean (verified implementation) lean-wnetkat, lean-wnetkat-opt docker/src/lean-wnetkat (Lean 4.33.1) KATch katch docker/src/katch (Scala 3) KATch2 katch2 docker/src/katch2 (Rust) McNetKAT mcnetkat , mcnetkat-ablation docker/src/mcnetkat (OCaml 4.10) Storm storm, storm-pnk upstream movesrwth/storm image Every engine prints its result on stdout as a STATS key=value … line and/or a verdict line; these are the fields recorded in original-results/. Source code The source code of every tool is in docker/src/, exactly as built into the images; docker/src/PROVENANCE.txt records each one’s git revision. docker/src/neko/: Neko, the paper’s tool, in Rust (src/, tests in tests/, usage in README.md). It builds neko and the ablation builds. docker/src/neko-networks/: the branch of Neko used for the case study and the synthetic benchmarks: the same code plus network generation in src/benchmark/ (fat-tree and Jellyfish topologies, ECMP and k-shortest routing, Parquet output), src/bin/benchmark_cdf.rs (neko-benchmark-cdf), and the trace-Pareto benchmarks in tests/ (neko-trace-bench). docker/src/lean-wnetkat/: the verified Lean 4 implementation: the wSPP definitions and operations (Wnetkat/Wspp/), their proofs (Wnetkat/Semantics/, e.g. Soundness.lean and Completeness.lean, and Wnetkat/Transport/), and the executables (Main.lean, MainOpt.lean, which are lean-wnetkat and lean-wnetkat-opt in the image). Base weighted NetKAT is vendored in vendor/WeightedNetKAT/. lake build in this directory checks every proof and builds both executables (Lean and Mathlib 4.33.1; see its README.md). docker/src/katch/, katch2/, mcnetkat/: the prior tools we compare against. Running the experiments Each class of experiment has one script in experiments/. Start with --quick, which runs a few small inputs in minutes; without it, a script runs the paper’s full input set. ./experiments/boolean.sh --quick ./experiments/probabilistic.sh --quick ./experiments/crossval.sh --quick ./experiments/ablation.sh --quick ./experiments/casestudy.sh --quick ./experiments/synthetic.sh --quick Script Reproduces Full run in our setup Compare with (original-results/) boolean.sh Fig. “Boolean reachability scalability”: Neko, Lean, KATch, KATch2 on 276 Topology Zoo networks 1.3 h boolean.csv probabilistic.sh Fig. “Probabilistic reachability scalability”: Neko, Lean, McNetKAT, Storm on 140 F10 and Bayonet policies 86 h, mostly Lean and Storm’s hybrid and dd engines hitting the 20 min limit probabilistic.csv crossval.sh “Correctness and Cross-Validation”: exact probabilities of sampled packet pairs, McNetKAT vs Neko vs Lean not recorded crossval_pairs.csv, crossval_raw/ ablation.sh “Ablation Experiments”: Neko with one optimization left out, on the 120 F10 policies 1.0 h ablation_loo.csv casestudy.sh Case study figures and table, and the witness-trace overhead: 50 seeds, with and without traces 24 h, up to 27 GiB of memory casestudy_timing.csv, casestudy_parquet/ synthetic.sh Appendix “Synthetic Adversarial Benchmarks” not recorded synthetic_width_scaling.csv, synthetic_netshape.csv Each script prints one line per run and a summary at the end, and writes results/ .csv; the full output of every run is kept in results/logs/. The boolean, probabilistic, crossval and ablation scripts give each run one CPU, 20 GB of memory and 20 minutes, as in the paper. Docker must be allowed at least that much memory (Docker Desktop: Settings > Resources); the case study needs about 28 GB. Options, for all scripts: - Input names run only those inputs, for example ./experiments/boolean.sh Abilene Kdl or ./experiments/probabilistic.sh bayonet/12_false. - --tools a,b runs only some tools. For example, ./experiments/probabilistic.sh --tools neko,mcnetkat,storm-sparse skips the slowest three. - --timeout S changes the per-run time limit. - --fresh discards earlier results. Without it, a re-run skips the runs already recorded, so an interrupted sweep continues where it stopped. Columns of the boolean, probabilistic and ablation CSVs: tool, input, size (nodes or switches), status (ok, timeout, oom, error), build_ms, peak_rss_kb, wall_s, and result (the reachability verdict, or E[delivered] for McNetKAT and Storm). To run one tool by hand: ./run.sh neko /data/topologyzoo/wnk/Abilene.wnk --wspp --r-reachability true. ./run.sh artifact-tools lists every tool in the image. Drawing the figures ./experiments/plot.sh # from results/ -> figures/results/ ./experiments/plot.sh original-results # from our cluster runs -> figures/original-results/ This draws the paper’s evaluation figures under the paper’s file names: bool_time.pdf, bool_mem.pdf, real_time.pdf, real_mem.pdf (with legends), loo_ablation_scatter.pdf, and the appendix’s f10_vs_jellyfish.pdf, trace_scaling_*.pdf and netshape_*.pdf. It also writes the numbers quoted in the text: agreement.txt (verdict agreement and exact cross-validation), ablation_summary.txt (slowdown per removed optimization) and casestudy_summary.txt (witness-trace overhead). The case study’s figure and table go to casestudy/: 3d-compact.pdf (Pareto-optimal points), switch-hotspot-curve.pdf (hotspot concentration), order-bars.pdf (network-to-network comparison), network-legend.pdf, and summary.csv (the summary table), plus the 3-D view from eight cameras (pareto3d- .pdf) and the data behind every figure as CSV. On the full case study this takes about 3 minutes and 9 GB of memory, and the CSV files take about 4 GB. experiments/casestudy_plots.py draws these from any Parquet files of the case study and has more options (python3 experiments/casestudy_plots.py --help), e.g. one figure per seed or --src/--dst to look at single host pairs. It works on partial results: each figure uses whatever runs exist, and an experiment with no results is skipped. Run on original-results/, it reproduces the paper’s figures. It runs on the host and needs Python 3 with matplotlib and numpy, and pyarrow, pyvista and pillow for the case study (python3 -m pip install matplotlib numpy pyarrow pyvista pillow; PYTHON=… selects another interpreter). Rebuilding the images cd docker ./build.sh arm64 # or amd64, or all; --save also writes ../images/*.tar.gz The images are built from the sources in docker/src/ (see Source code). docker/stage.sh (authors only) refreshes src/ from the development checkouts. docker/bin/ holds the small wrapper scripts installed in the image (katch, mcnetkat, mcnetkat-ablation, storm-pnk, artifact-tools). Build notes: the Storm base image (Ubuntu 25.10) ships Rust coreutils, whose timeout never kills the child, so the image switches to GNU coreutils. Lean’s -march=native is replaced by a portable baseline for each architecture. McNetKAT carries small source compatibility patches for its OCaml library versions (see docker/Dockerfile).

It runs on the host and needs Python 3 with matplotlib and numpy, and pyarrow, pyvista and pillow for the case study (python3 -m pip install matplotlib numpy pyarrow pyvista pillow; PYTHON=… selects another interpreter). Rebuilding the images cd docker ./build.sh arm64 # or amd64, or all; --save also writes ../images/*.tar.gz The images are built from the sources in docker/src/ (see Source code). docker/stage.sh (authors only) refreshes src/ from the development checkouts. docker/bin/ holds the small wrapper scripts installed in the image (katch, mcnetkat, mcnetkat-ablation, storm-pnk, artifact-tools). Build notes: the Storm base image (Ubuntu 25.10) ships Rust coreutils, whose timeout never kills the child, so the image switches to GNU coreutils. Lean’s -march=native is replaced by a portable baseline for each architecture. McNetKAT carries small source compatibility patches for its OCaml library versions (see docker/Dockerfile).

title: Representing student history for knowledge tracing in Finnish language and literature
abstract: This study asks how much of a student’s previous performance must be retained topredict what the student will do next. We analyzed 19,827,938 Finnish language andliterature responses from 46,021 students in Grades 4–6. Students were entirely separatedbetween training, validation, and test sets. Prediction from item identity alone achieved a testAUC of .8241. Adding a single recency-weighted measure of previous performance increasedAUC to .8732 and reduced log loss from .4446 to .3883. Expanding the explicit student statefrom one to 100 dimensions produced only a small improvement, increasing test AUC from.8732 to .8739. A 128-dimensional transformer that learned one common summary of thestudent’s previous responses achieved a test AUC of .8978 and log loss of .3513. Atransformer that allowed each target item to select information directly from previousresponses improved performance further, to an AUC of .9153 and log loss of .3228. Theresults show that Finnish learning histories can be compressed substantially, but richerlearned representations retain considerably more predictive information than a singleperformance measure, and prediction improves further when different information can beretrieved for different target items.

title: Interpretable and Trustworthy AI for Medical Imaging Analysis Beyond Post Hoc Justifications
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated remarkable potential in medical imag-ing analysis, but its lack of interpretability and trust remains a central challenge to clini-cal adoption. This thesis explores a series of projects that aim to make medical AI in-terpretable and trustworthy by design rather than through post hoc justifications, focus-ing on both the reasoning process of the models and their alignment with pathology. We begin with a study on breast cancer segmentation using dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), where we leverage the heart as an anatomical anchor. The heart’s structural and signal stability across patients makes it a reliable internal refer-ence. By analyzing correlations between the heart and nearby tissues, we can estimate patient-level certainty by predicting false positives and false negatives—particularly those caused by image degradations and dataset bias. This approach transforms ana-tomical consistency into a built-in verification tool, illustrating how region-specific sta-bility can serve as a source of model certainty and error prediction. The next project addresses machine-agnostic segmentation of COVID-19 lesions, as dataset bias is a major concern for model trustworthiness. Here, we collected multi-national data (from China and Saudi Arabia) spanning five different hospitals and sev-en scanning protocols. We then developed a simulation algorithm based on modeled pathological processes and scanning settings, and a 2.5D model that minimizes the ef-fect of dataset bias. This design improves model trust, as it is highly robust against var-iations caused by patient populations and scanning conditions. Building on this, we developed an AI pipeline to detect sub-visual lesions in COVID-19 survivors with long-term respiratory symptoms. These lesions, invisible to radiologists, were uncovered through a modular, interpretable workflow. Each module extracted features with clear pathological meaning, and the final predictions were cross-validated against both clinical outcomes and spatial lung distribution patterns. This de-sign convinced physicians that the findings were trustworthy—even though they could not directly observe the features themselves. Together, these projects outline a unified path toward interpretable and trustworthy AI in medical imaging through embedding verifiability and medical logic into the mod-el’s structure, training, and workflow design.

title: On Making $\mathrm{SE}(2)$-Invariant Networks Optimal
abstract: Respecting a-priori known symmetries of underlying data is a key principle in designing efficient neural architectures. Convolutional neural networks are a canonical example, encoding translation equivariance. Extending this inductive bias to richer symmetry groups such as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ in the most effective way possible is an ongoing architectural and computational challenge. Building on classical invariant theory, we derive invariant feature maps that are provably optimal: minimal and information-preserving with respect to the symmetry group. Our construction is designed to integrate seamlessly into standard architectures, requiring no modification to nonlinearities or normalization layers. As a concrete implementation, we introduce a plug-and-play module for convolutional neural networks that enforces $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ invariance, capturing both translations and rotations within standard architectures. The resulting models are both efficient and expressive. Experiments show competitive or improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art equivariant methods at significantly lower computational cost. Finally, we provide a theoretical and empirical analysis of the relationship between equivariance and invariance, offering insight into their roles in controlling robustness and flexibility.

title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

title: Topic Transformer
abstract: Text classification models often rely on transformer-based embeddings or topic modeling 2 techniques independently, limiting their ability to capture both contextual and thematic 3 information. We propose the Topic-Transformer (TT) framework, a multi-view learning 4 framework that combines transformer-based encoders and topic modeling methods to 5 improve text classification performance. TT processes text simultaneously through a 6 transformer model and a topic modeling technique. The resulting contextual embeddings 7 and topic representations are then fed into a classification head. TT is tested using five 8 distinct transformer encoders and three topic modeling techniques, resulting in fifteen 9 configurations of TT. The tests are conducted on six benchmark datasets and the results 10 are evaluated in terms of macro-average F1-score, precision, recall, and training time. The 11 results indicate that TT outperforms standalone transformers across all datasets. Most 12 notably, the benefit of incorporating topic representations becomes increasingly apparent 13 as dataset complexity rises, in terms of vocabulary, sequence length among others. As in 14 the simplest dataset, the results improved between 0.1% and 0.4% on average in terms 15 of macro-average F1-score, whereas, in the most complex one, the increase ranged from 16 1.3% to 3.3% in the same metric. Our findings highlight the complementary nature of 17 transformer-based and topic modeling approaches, indicating that hybrid architectures can 18 improve performance in Natural Language Processing tasks. title: Large Language Models for Cybersecurity in the Quantum Era: A Critical Review of Trustworthy AI, Emerging Threats, and Post-Quantum Defense
abstract: The convergence of two disruptive forces — large-scale foundation models (large languagemodels, LLMs, and multimodal systems) and the maturing threat of quantum computing — is reshaping cybersecurityfrom both the defensive and offensive sides. Large models are being embedded into security operations, vulnerabilitydiscovery, and threat-intelligence pipelines, while quantum algorithms threaten to invalidate the public-key infrastructureunderlying nearly all deployed cryptographic protocols. Despite an explosion of publications in both areas, the literatureremains fragmented: AI-for-security research rarely engages with post-quantum considerations, and post-quantumcryptography (PQC) research rarely engages with the trustworthiness failures of the AI systems that will manage themigration. Methods. This paper conducts a critical, structured review synthesizing evidence from AI security, systemssecurity, and post-quantum cryptography literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026. We construct a multidimensional taxonomy of AI-for-cybersecurity paradigms, systematize large-model-specific trustworthiness failures —adversarial robustness, data poisoning, prompt injection, model extraction, hallucination, and supply-chain risk — andmap the intersection between AI-enabled defense and AI-assisted post-quantum migration. Key findings. Reportedperformance gains for LLM-based security tools are frequently measured on narrow, contamination-prone benchmarksthat do not reflect adversarial, non-stationary production environments. Prompt injection remains structurally unsolvedrather than merely under-mitigated: reported task-hijacking success rates against tool-using agents rise sharply onceattackers tailor techniques to agent-specific behavior. Offensive robustness evaluation lags defensive-capability evaluationby roughly an order of magnitude in surveyed agentic-security papers. AI-assisted tooling for PQC migration —cryptographic discovery, code auditing, risk scoring — is nascent and inherits the reliability problems of the underlyingmodels it is built on. Implications. We argue the two challenges are entangled rather than parallel: securing the migrationto quantum-resistant cryptography will depend on AI-assisted automation at a scale classical tooling cannot match, yetthat automation must be trusted under exactly the adversarial conditions where current large models are weakest. Weclose with a prioritized research agenda spanning evaluation methodology, quantum-aware threat modeling, and cryptoagility tooling for 2026–2035.Index Terms—artificial intelligence; cybersecurity; large language models; adversarial machine learning; promptinjection; post-quantum cryptography; quantum computing; trustworthy AI; security operations; AI red teaming

title: Replication package for "Solving the Wrong Structure Right: Local LLM Agents for Disposable Engineering Computation"
abstract: This dataset accompanies the article "Solving the Wrong Structure Right: Local LLM Agents for Disposable Engineering Computation". It contains the complete record of a campaign in which local open-weight LLM agents, running on a single workstation, wrote single-use solvers for five plane-truss problems: 510 runs across three agent harnesses, two models and two prompt formulations. Contents:- 01_tasks: the task files exactly as the agents received them (inputs, descriptions, the visible verifier, both prompts), with the script and the Ftool models from which the cases were built.- 02_references: the reference solution of each case, withheld from the agents and used only by the evaluator.- 03_runs: every run, with the agent's complete workspace, its log, wall-clock time, exit code and Python environment, and the sampling parameters reported by the inference server.- 04_tools: the evaluation scripts, and the scores recorded in the blind assessment of the figures.

title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.

title: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers
abstract: Emotions are expressed on a continuum and are naturally described in the valence-arousal (VA) space. Existing VA-based image editors are typically training-based and domain-specific, limiting them to VA regions seen during training and making them brittle across datasets and domains. Meanwhile, despite producing high-quality edits, state-of-the-art foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers: non-linear emotion representations in text encoders makes prompt interpolation poorly calibrated, so accurate and continuous VA control remains unreliable. To fill this gap, we introduce Barycentric Guidance, a training-free framework that turns pretrained foundation image editors into continuous affective controllers over VA, requiring no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. Our method maps any target VA point to simplex-based guidance weights, enabling VA controllability in three aspects: (i) accurate targeting of VA states, (ii) broad coverage across the VA plane, and (iii) continuous control. Across three face datasets, we improve VA target accuracy by 25-29%, expand VA-plane coverage by 28-50%, and increase expression diversity by 29-49%, over the strongest baseline. Unlike prior domain-specific methods, our training-free approach exploits the foundation model's inherent versatility, enabling generalization beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework. Code is available at https://github.com/harveymannering/BarycentricGuidance.

title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. Across sixteen designs and seven LLMs, a single-iteration study compares three agent control granularities - expert-written recipes, direct EDA operations and LLM-constructed procedures - to ask how much control an agent needs per attempt. Functional-pass rates are 98.2%, 71.4% and 17.9%, respectively; yet direct operations give slightly larger 3.4% median Fmax gains when passing, versus 3.2% for recipes. This exposes a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Informed by this trade-off, a multi-iteration study fixes the action tier at expert recipes to ask how repeated attempts are best organised, comparing a fitted deterministic heuristic with sequential LLM reasoning, branching exploration and knowledge base-guided exploration within 12 checkpoints per run. Branching raises mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential) to 16.0%, and the knowledge base to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs. Characterisation across 2,421 recipe attempts profiled their gain and validation rates, showing hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain at 41.4MHz.

title: Throwing4: Phase-Aware Pose Modeling for Throw-Distance Prediction in Elite Athletics
abstract: Elite athletics throwing provides a structured biomechanical action sequence together with an objective continuous outcome, namely throw distance, making it a suitable setting for performance-oriented sports analytics. In this work, we investigate whether explicit phase alignment of pose dynamics improves throw-distance prediction under realistic broadcast conditions. To support this study, we curate Throwing4, a dataset of 500 elite throwing clips spanning javelin, discus, hammer, and shot put, with corresponding two-dimensional pose sequences, frame-level phase annotations, and official distance labels. We formulate throw-distance prediction from broadcast-derived pose as a regression problem and compare full-sequence modeling against a phase-conditioned approach that partitions each attempt into four technique stages and fuses phase-specific motion representations. Experiments across multiple graph-based pose encoders show a consistent reduction in prediction error when phase structure is incorporated, indicating that phase-aligned modeling provides a more stable representation than treating the entire motion as an unstructured sequence. These findings suggest that explicit biomechanical phase information is a useful inductive prior for pose-based performance modeling in elite athletics throwing. Beyond score prediction, the dataset and protocol provide a basis for future work on fine-grained technique analysis, interpretable sports analytics, and robust modeling from broadcast video.

title: XForecast: The KDD 2026 Finance Day Challenge on News-Grounded Financial Forecasting
abstract: Financial forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical time-series (TS) signals, while textual information such as news remains largely underutilized. We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting, where the task is to predict stock price movements four weeks ahead using both historical price data and paired news signals. XForecast combines stock price data with curated financial text generated using FinTexTS, a multimodal dataset generation method. It covers 100 large-cap stocks from 2019--2023, with training on 2019--2022 and evaluation on 2023. To better evaluate models that leverage textual signals, we adopt a weighted hit rate metric that places greater emphasis on instances where news information is expected to have stronger influence. The XForecast Challenge, hosted on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, aims to benchmark methods for integrating financial TS and textual information.

title: Interaksi AI Dan Mediatisasi Antarmuka Dalam Pembelian Impulsif Gen Z Di Shopee Melalui Media Equation
abstract: Latar belakang: Perkembangan Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan mediatisasi antarmuka pada platform e-commerce telah mengubah pola interaksi digital Generasi Z dan berpotensi mendorong pembelian impulsif. Dalam konteks ini, Media Equation menjelaskan kecenderungan pengguna merespons AI sebagai entitas sosial ketika teknologi menghadirkan interaksi yang menyerupai manusia. Tujuan: Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis pengaruh Interaksi AI dan Mediatisasi Antarmuka terhadap Pembelian Impulsif pada Generasi Z pengguna Shopee serta menguji peran Media Equation dalam hubungan tersebut. Metode: Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif eksplanatori dengan desain survei cross-sectional. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner daring dari 396 responden Generasi Z yang memenuhi kriteria penelitian dan dianalisis menggunakan Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Hasil: Interaksi AI berpengaruh positif dan signifikan terhadap Pembelian Impulsif (β = 0,202; T = 3,480; p = 0,001), sedangkan Mediatisasi Antarmuka tidak berpengaruh signifikan secara langsung (β = −0,066; T = 0,862; p = 0,389). Pengaruh tidak langsung melalui Media Equation signifikan pada hubungan Interaksi AI dengan Pembelian Impulsif (β = 0,154; T = 5,501; p < 0,001) dan Mediatisasi Antarmuka dengan Pembelian Impulsif (β = 0,137; T = 4,846; p < 0,001). Kesimpulan: Temuan menunjukkan bahwa pembelian impulsif Generasi Z lebih kuat dipengaruhi oleh kualitas interaksi AI dan terbentuknya persepsi sosial terhadap AI dibandingkan kualitas antarmuka secara langsung. Media Equation menjadi mekanisme psikologis penting yang menghubungkan pengalaman digital dengan perilaku pembelian impulsif.

title: Utility-Aware Occupancy Camouflage for Point Cloud Privacy: Pilot Release
abstract: Code and per-frame numerical results for a scoped pilot on utility-aware occupancy camouflage: a deterministic, gradient-free sender-side defense that removes the lowest-utility fraction of occupied voxels in order to degrade an occupancy-based point-cloud reconstruction path. Released artifacts cover a fixed 16-frame KITTI Velodyne subset across nine removal budgets. A journal-independent package additionally reproduces the manuscript's occupancy-entropy analysis across ten removal budgets, including the released figure and tables.

title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures — code, reports and trained adapters
abstract: Code, configurations, episode logs, reports and trained LoRA adapters for the paper "Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures" (Zavattari, Tommasi, Prencipe, 2026; preprint). The archive is the GitHub repository https://github.com/bradstallion/interventions-as-labels at its release snapshot of 2026-10-12, with the 34 trained LoRA adapters added under store/derived/*/adapter/. The adapters are needed only to re-evaluate the edited models of the paper without retraining them; everything else, including the recomputation of every table and figure from the released reports, runs from the GitHub repository alone. See README.md inside the archive for setup (uv sync --all-extras) and for what each directory contains. Code: MIT license. Data, reports and documents: CC BY 4.0.

title: Hybrid feature selection framework for reliable solar irradiance prediction using ground-based meteorological data
abstract: Accurate solar irradiance (SI) prediction is essential for optimizing solar energy (SE) generation and improving the reliability of renewable energy systems. However, the complex and nonlinear interactions among meteorological variables often limit the performance and interpretability of conventional forecasting models. The main challenge addressed in this study is the reliable identification of physically meaningful predictors under nonlinear, non-normal, multicollinear, and sensor-sensitive meteorological conditions. This study develops a reliability-aware feature evaluation framework that integrates established statistical, nonlinear, and explainable methods to assess ground-based meteorological predictors under non-normal, multicollinear, and sensor-sensitive conditions. Linear relationships between predictors were first examined using Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation analyses together with principal component analysis (PCA) to identify dominant variance structures. Nonlinear feature sensitivity was then evaluated using a bilayer neural network, while SHAP and LIME techniques were applied to provide global and local interpretability of model predictions. The results indicate that average battery voltage (ABV) is the most influential predictor of SI (RMSE = 0.203), followed by relative humidity (RMSE = 0.239) and wind direction (RMSE = 0.244). PCA results show that the first three principal components explain 62.88% of the total variance in the dataset. Explainability analysis further confirms that ABV and RH contribute most significantly to SI prediction, while rainfall exhibits minimal global influence due to its sparse occurrence. The framework improves understanding of nonlinear meteorological interactions and supports reliability-aware predictor evaluation for SI modelling. The findings provide valuable insights for SE planning, smart grid integration, and sustainable renewable energy management.
