title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
abstract: Agentic workflows combine large language models with planning, memory, tools, execution environments, and iterative feedback. Their failures are difficult to diagnose because the same user-visible symptom may originate from model behavior, workflow orchestration, external tools, infrastructure, or their interaction. This paper presents a source-aware taxonomy of agentic workflow failures and applies it to evidence from academic literature and GitHub. The taxonomy combines source attribution with three empirical dimensions: a concrete failure-type dictionary, workflow-stage localization, and agent-capability localization. Its central structure is a two-axis localization matrix: workflow stages form the horizontal process axis and agent capabilities form the vertical functional axis. This design moves beyond taxonomies that mainly classify final failure manifestations by localizing intermediate process states inside agent operation. Our empirical comparison shows that literature-derived failures emphasize planning, reasoning, learning, perception, and knowledge-related mechanisms, whereas GitHub-derived failures concentrate on execution-stage, actuation-related, tool, API, and infrastructure failures. The dominant hotspot is iterative execution and actuation. These findings indicate that agentic workflow reliability should be treated as a systems problem rather than only a model-output problem. The taxonomy provides a basis for structured evaluation, root cause analysis, failure injection, and engineering triage.

title: Implicit and explicit reparameterizations of the Folded Normal and Rice distributions
abstract: Variational inference is a flexible tool for modeling experimental data and has proven useful in crystallography. Pathwise gradient estimators provide low-variance gradients for reparameterized variational inference, but are not readily available for some distributions central to crystallography. This work derives and implements implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in \prog{PyTorch}, and compares their variance analytically and empirically. In each case the implicit estimator achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios, while the scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. For both distributions, implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger. As a practical application, French-Wilson scaling is formulated as a variational inference problem, using the folded Normal and Rice distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, respectively. Both estimators recover the exact posterior to better than $1\%$ on the amplitude, and converge at the same rate. The implementations are available in the open-source package \prog{rs-distributions}.

title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

title: Adaptive Interaction Network for Human Motion Prediction During Human-Robot Collaboration
abstract: Human motion prediction during human-robot collaboration is critical for achieving safe and efficient interactions in shared environments. Unlike previous studies that have primarily focused on humans and objects, we focus on the robot-aware human motion prediction task, which explicitly models the influence of robots on human motion. This task presents new challenges, such as capturing human-robot heterogeneity and modeling complex spatial interactions. To address these issues, we develop an adaptive interaction network (AINet) model that consists of two branches: a primary branch that predicts future human motion and an auxiliary branch that estimates robot trajectories. The two branches are jointly optimized and coupled via a Local-Global Spatial Interaction (LGSI) Module, which effectively captures fine-grained and global contextual dependencies between human and robot motion sequences. Then, we introduce an Adaptive Weighted Aggregation (AWA) Module to dynamically fuse motion features using context-dependent weights, thereby increasing adaptability across diverse scenarios. Furthermore, we adopt a coarse-to-fine prediction strategy, in which a coarse pseudo-trajectory is first predicted, followed by the refinement of detailed human poses based on that trajectory. Extensive experiments on three challenging datasets reveal that our proposed method achieves superior performance, validating its effectiveness in human-robot collaboration scenarios. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LyTingHub/AINet.

title: PersonaFactor: Preference Factors with Dynamic Selection for LLM Personalization
abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.

title: HAKEM: Multilingual Spoken-Item Selection Without Transcription
abstract: Research preprint; not peer reviewed. HAKEM studies multilingual spoken-item selection from a supplied typed catalogue using frozen speech models. It scores each candidate under teacher forcing and subtracts its matched digital-silence score, without task-specific weight training, candidate speech enrolment or a pronunciation lexicon. The main read-aloud Hassaniya study evaluates 2,892 recordings from 16 speakers against 1,491 catalogue rows. Frozen Whisper tiny achieves 96.6% top-1 selection, compared with 65.6% for transcription followed by catalogue matching. The paper also reports a 22-language extension, simulated channel/noise experiments, a 400-clip English phrase-selection comparison, and an exploratory 853-clip low-resource rewarded-beam extension. The results concern closed-catalogue selection with the correct item supplied. They do not establish full speech-transcription accuracy, spontaneous ordered-command understanding, universal language coverage or world-best performance. The manuscript discloses protocol amendments, failed original criteria, generation failures and reproduction limitations. Hassaniya recordings will remain private and will not be distributed with the paper. Private catalogue rows and identities are not redistributed; other data can be shared only under their applicable licences and release rights. The author confirms speaker agreement to research use and publication of findings while Hassaniya recordings remain private. Some main-study checkpoint and fine-tune lineage remain unresolved. Internal manuscript version: Draft 6.

The manuscript discloses protocol amendments, failed original criteria, generation failures and reproduction limitations. Hassaniya recordings will remain private and will not be distributed with the paper. Private catalogue rows and identities are not redistributed; other data can be shared only under their applicable licences and release rights. The author confirms speaker agreement to research use and publication of findings while Hassaniya recordings remain private. Some main-study checkpoint and fine-tune lineage remain unresolved. title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.

title: Quantum integration in Besov spaces with mixed smoothness
abstract: We study the complexity of high-dimensional integration of periodic functions from Besov spaces $S^r_{p,q}B(\mathbb{T}^d)$ with mixed smoothness in the quantum model of computation. We construct new quantum algorithms based on the multivariate Faber-Schauder decomposition of such functions and analyze their convergence rates. We show a gain of one convergence order compared to the well-known deterministic rates of convergence. We additionally obtain lower bounds showing the optimality of our results up to logarithms.

title: SCOPE Before You Sample: Conformal Scores Guide Posterior Exploration for Fast and Calibrated Bayesian Predictive Inference
abstract: Bayesian predictive regions account for parameter uncertainty but can be poorly calibrated under model misspecification, even with expensive full MCMC. Cheaper approximations such as variational inference reduce the cost but often yield less accurate predictive distributions. We propose SCOPE (Score-guided Conformal Posterior Exploration), which retains the predictive quality of full MCMC while achieving calibrated coverage at a fraction of its cost. The key observation is that a prediction region can depend on the posterior mainly through a few parameter directions that move the region's boundary, and these are generally not the directions of largest posterior variance. SCOPE gives nonconformity scores a new role in guiding posterior computation: score gradients on a held-out guide set, weighted toward the target boundary, identify the relevant directions. MCMC explores this subspace, while an inexpensive projected variational approximation carries the remaining uncertainty. The same guide set calibrates the region's final density level. We establish asymptotic coverage for SCOPE and provide a split variant with finite-sample validity. Controlled simulations show that score-guided exploration yields more accurate calibrated regions than non-targeted direction choices at low active rank. Across simulated and real benchmarks, SCOPE has a median test-NLL gap of only 0.002 nats relative to full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and on the real benchmarks it runs 12-15 times faster.

title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).

title: Rule vs.Consequence: Dissociable Internal Representations of Moral Reasoning in LLMs
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. We construct a 2$\times$2 factorial dataset crossing reasoning style (rule-based vs. consequence-based framing) with judgment polarity (permissive vs. prohibitive), drawn from three established moral reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on a cleanroom test set of novel phrasings that includes conflict pairs where the two framings predict opposite labels. Using linear probing and activation steering, we identify two orthogonal directions in the residual stream: Dir-A tracks reasoning style and Dir-B tracks judgment polarity, each near-blind to the other factor (cross-correlation $|r| < 0.04$). This double dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models from different developers at comparable proportional depth, and it is not knife-edged in layer: the directions are recoverable and causally effective throughout an extended band of the network. Dir-A can causally change judgments, and in conflicting scenarios, it selectively corrects errors in rule-based judgments without changing consequence-based judgments, suggesting that it does not simply make the model more likely to accept everything. Generalization beyond the training templates is partial: the direction transfers across benchmark sources, but its advantage over lexical baselines on novel phrasings is modest. We therefore frame the result as moral reasoning style sensitivity, a geometrically dissociable and causally effective structure, rather than internalized normative reasoning.

title: MammoDiff: weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection via classifier-guided denoising diffusion models—a real-world clinical study on the KHCC mammography cohort
abstract: Introduction Early detection of malignant mammographic lesions is a critical clinical challenge, particularly where large annotated datasets are unavailable. Supervised deep learning achieves near-radiologist performance but requires large datasets with reliable labels and pixel/ROI annotations. Weakly supervised anomaly detection, requiring only image-level binary labels, offers an annotation-efficient alternative, yet prior GAN- and autoencoder-based methods have struggled to preserve fine anatomical detail in the mammographic domain. Methods We present MammoDiff, to our knowledge the first application of classifier-guided denoising diffusion models to weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection, trained and evaluated on 3,013 mammograms from 806 patients at King Hussein Cancer Center (KHCC), Jordan. MammoDiff encodes input anatomy through deterministic DDIM noise encoding and reconstructs a counterfactual healthy image guided by the gradient signal of a noise-conditioned binary classifier. The anomaly map is the pixel-wise absolute difference between input and reconstruction, and the image-level score is obtained by spatial mean pooling. A 3 × 3 ablation over noise level L ∈ {250, 500, 750} and gradient scale s ∈ {50, 100, 200} was performed on the validation set. Results The optimal configuration ( L = 750, s = 50) achieved AUROC = 0.7246 [95% CI: 0.6685, 0.7825] on the held-out test set ( n = 304), compared with a simplified PatchCore-style baseline (AUROC = 0.6634) and a supervised ResNet-50 reference (AUROC = 0.8100), without pixel-level annotation. The proposed Healthy-Shift Index (HSI) was positive for 94.8% of malignant and 87.4% of normal cases, so it is the separation between the class distributions rather than the sign of the index that carries information. Discussion This performance is not clinically deployable: at the Youden-optimal threshold the sensitivity is 0.6013, meaning that 61 of 153 malignant cases are missed, well below the approximately 87% targeted by FDA-cleared triage devices, and the study is single-centre without external validation. MammoDiff is therefore presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and a reproducible baseline for future work, not as a screening or triage tool..

title: Adversarial Robustness Enhancement through Deep Feature Representations-Based CIFAR-10 Image Classification
abstract: Adversarial perturbations pose a significant challenge to the reliability of deep neural networks in image classification. The conventional feature aggregation approaches are still vulnerable to adversarial noise, which inspires the improvement of more powerful feature presentations. In this study, the adversarial robustness of a ResNet34-based architecture is investigated on the CIFAR-10 dataset, where conventional global average pooling (GAP) is compared with a proposed framework combines Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Fractal Average Pooling (FAP) within a ResNet-34. Multiple perturbation budgets were tested on the models via the white-box fast gradient sign method (FGSM) and projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks. The test accuracy of the proposed model was 97.52% on clean data whereas the test accuracy of the GAP baseline was 95.69%, which is a 1.83% improvement. In the FGSM, the adversarial accuracy increased from 59.56% to 81.38% at e = 1/255 and from 15.81% to 70.81% at e = 8/255. With the PGD, the improvement was not significant; the accuracy increased from 0.06% to 14.99% at e = 1/255 but reached only 0.32% versus 0.03% at e = 8/255. The distortion characteristics of any of the above methods are highly similar to the perturbation-quality analysis results of the PSNR, SSIM, SNR, and MSE. Overall, the proposed representation enhances the ability to perform clean classification tasks while also being robust to FGSM attacks, while stronger iterative PGD attacks are still a major challenge

title: Multiple Digital Signature Integration in the University Data Backup Archive using Enhanced DLP-based Security Framework
abstract: The dependency of universities on information systems has emphasized the need for a secure archival mechanism for institutional data. This study covers the implementation of a repository for database backup of Bicol University using a multiple digital signatory framework using Enhanced Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP). The method consolidates five security managers of Bicol University, each maintaining their own digital signatures. The backup activity covers hashing of the database files using SHA-512 and encrypts the result using an Enhanced DLP-based Cryptosystem to generate a consolidated digital signature. The verification process requires the participation of, but is not limited to, five (5) security managers to ensure integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation of the backup file and the stored security stamp. The evaluation conducted showed consistent and validated generation of digital signatures and security stamps, reliable detection of file tampering, and integration of collaborative authorization of security managers, which establishes distributed accountability and operational trust. Further analysis of the algorithm showed no established patterns between the plaintext and ciphertext, manifesting a high level of security. The sensitivity test using the Avalanche Effect exposed no patterns between the ciphertext and the plaintext and key, manifesting encryption strength. This was further validated by the use of the Strict Avalanche Criterion (SAC), which also showed a higher level of security. However, complexity analysis disclosed that higher computing resources are necessary to effectively implement the system. Nonetheless, the study confirmed that the enhanced DLP-based multiple digital signature framework is cryptographically secured and provides a practical and scalable approach for securing institutional data.

title: Beyond Topic Matching: Goal-Conditioned Evaluation of Research Contributions in ETD Collections
abstract: Evaluating whether scholarly research contributes to a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) requires an interpretive framework that combines the goal definition, its targets, contribution criteria, and the document itself. Instruction-tuned large language models can instantiate this framework in context, producing a consistent evaluative function that can be applied to every document in a collection. We present Goal-Conditioned Multi-Label Distillation (GCMLD), which distills this evaluative function into a compact multi-label model. A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct teacher evaluates each document–SDG pair by constraining its generative output to two tokens ("0" and "1"), and the logit margin defines the teacher probability used to supervise the student. An 86-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3-base student learns to approximate the teacher’s evaluative function by predicting all seventeen SDG scores in a single model invocation. We test whether reducing the influence of intermediate teacher evaluations improves or impairs approximation by comparing plain binary cross-entropy with weighting, masking, and hard-label objectives. Masking small-margin evaluations reduced teacher fidelity with the teacher targets and temperature held fixed, and the reduction was largest for SDG–document pairs whose own margins are small. The loss of fidelity shows that intermediate teacher evaluations provide useful supervision for approximating the evaluative function. The student trained on publication abstracts continued to approximate the teacher on electronic thesis and dissertation (ETD) abstracts, with ETD-specific distillation producing modest additional gains. Replacing seventeen prompted teacher evaluations with one model invocation makes collection-scale evaluation practical. Aggregating document-level contribution probabilities by academic department demonstrates how the distilled model supports collection-scale analysis of institutional research.

title: Ant colony optimization plus temporal difference and opposition-based learning for semi-supervised multi-label feature selection
abstract: This paper presents a novel feature selection method for multi-label data, combining Ant Colony Optimization with Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Opposition-Based Learning in a semi-supervised framework. Ant colony optimization navigates the feature space, while RL dynamically updates heuristic functions to predict rewards for selected features. Opposition-Based Learning enhances exploration by evaluating both original and complementary solutions. The semi-supervised learning aspect allows the algorithm to leverage the structure of the unlabeled data, improving the quality of feature selection even when labeled data is scarce. For the first time, the impact of the proposed algorithm has been systematically investigated. Compared to baseline methods, the approach achieves 7% and 3% relative improvement in Accuracy, 6% and 4% relative reduction in Hamming loss with 20% and 40% labeled data. Evaluated on 8 datasets using the Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors classifier, the method outperforms traditional techniques by refining feature subsets through unlabeled data. The method’s higher computational complexity and memory requirements compared to baseline techniques make it better suited for high-accuracy tasks where real-time processing is not critical, such as precision-driven biomedical analysis or batch-oriented industrial data mining. This work establishes a new benchmark for semi-supervised multi-label feature selection, prioritizing accuracy in scenarios where computational latency is tolerable.

title: MAPLE: manifold-aligned purification with logit-edge calibration for robust black-box adversarial defense
abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in visual recognition tasks, yet they remain highly vulnerable to adversarial examples. Existing black-box defenses are mainly based on input transformation, including denoising and purification networks that attempt to remove adversarial perturbations before classification. However, their effectiveness is limited by the complexity of high-dimensional image manifolds and the difficulty of perfectly recovering clean images. To address this issue, this paper proposes MAPLE (Manifold-Aligned Purification with Logit-Edge Calibration), a robust black-box adversarial defense framework that jointly enhances semantic purification and margin calibration. MAPLE consists of a Semantic Purification Network (SPN), implemented as a fully convolutional purification network, and a Margin Calibration Classifier (MCC), initialized from the target classifier. During training, the MCC first guides the SPN to purify adversarial examples into classification-consistent images. Then, the trained SPN provides purified adversarial examples for MCC calibration, allowing the classifier to reshape its local decision geometry around residual adversarial regions. These two phases are performed through cyclic co-calibration, enabling the defense pipeline to progressively suppress adversarial perturbations while enlarging the local classification margin. evidence.title: MAPLE: manifold-aligned purification with logit-edge calibration for robust black-box adversarial defense
evidence.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in visual recognition tasks, yet they remain highly vulnerable to adversarial examples. Existing black-box defenses are mainly based on input transformation, including denoising and purification networks that attempt to remove adversarial perturbations before classification. However, their effectiveness is limited by the complexity of high-dimensional image manifolds and the difficulty of perfectly recovering clean images. To address this issue, this paper proposes MAPLE (Manifold-Aligned Purification with Logit-Edge Calibration), a robust black-box adversarial defense framework that jointly enhances semantic purification and margin calibration. MAPLE consists of a Semantic Purification Network (SPN), implemented as a fully convolutional purification network, and a Margin Calibration Classifier (MCC), initialized from the target classifier. During training, the MCC first guides the SPN to purify adversarial examples into classification-consistent images. Then, the trained SPN provides purified adversarial examples for MCC calibration, allowing the classifier to reshape its local decision geometry around residual adversarial regions. These two phases are performed through cyclic co-calibration, enabling the defense pipeline to progressively suppress adversarial perturbations while enlarging the local classification margin. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and Mini-ImageNet demonstrate that MAPLE consistently outperforms previous mainstream methods under diverse black-box attacks, providing an effective and practical defense paradigm for transferable adversarial attacks.

title: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
abstract: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.

title: Foundations for a Lens of Quantum Governance
abstract: The second quantum revolution is a revolution of information. Advances in quantum computation, communication, and sensing offer new capabilities while raising questions about how quantum infrastructures will be organised, accessed, and governed. We argue that their significance for governance lies not in transforming political principles, but in how their technical and infrastructural requirements may affect existing relationships of authority, responsibility, legitimacy, and power. This paper develops a quantum governance lens that connects governance scholarship with quantum information science, examining interactions between technical design, institutional arrangements, and infrastructural dependencies. We apply this lens to five areas: quantum computation, quantum key distribution, Quantum Byzantine Agreement, blind quantum computation, and dual-use quantum sensing. These applications illustrate how technical capabilities may influence access, trust, privacy, oversight, and accountability, while demonstrating that technical guarantees cannot resolve institutional questions independently. We conclude that quantum technologies do not necessarily introduce unique governance challenges or require entirely new governance frameworks. Rather, they provide a context in which established questions of legitimacy, accountability, and equity must be reconsidered in relation to emerging technological capabilities and institutional choices.

title: Weak Segmentation-Guided GAN for~Realistic Color Edition
abstract: Editing the color of images in a realistic way finds many applications such as changing the perception of an image, data augmentation or film post processing. The design of an automatic tool is a complex and long addressed challenge. In particular, two properties are difficult to meet altogether: generating realistic results without artifacts and the possibility to precisely choose the future color. Conventional methods using segmentation and histogram matching maximize the controllability but also introduce a lack of realism or are complex to automate. On the contrary, GANs that specialize in realism are difficult to control. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel GAN architecture leveraging any differentiable segmentation model. We demonstrate the genericness of our framework that presents state of the art results on different use cases. It generates images that look realistic while offering a precise color control.

title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].

title: Model Scale versus Search in Novel Mathematical Problem Solving: An Exploratory Comparison of Ministral 3.5 and GPT Frontier Models
abstract: The purpose of this study is to investigate the importance of model scale in solving challenging mathematical problems, identifying the four most significant elements: learnt model scale, computational time expectation, search diversity, and verification. Results from the harder twenty problem set saw the Ministral 3.5 comparator obtain 19/20 while the GPT counterpart got 16/20, pointing towards the possibility of lower-scale models being able to solve many hard problems. However, the outcome was different when examining 5 constant problems, with Ministral proving correct in 3/5 cases, but failing in a logarithmic integral (T9) and constrained global optimization (T18), while the later GPT model was accurate on all 5 problems. The use of repeated search methods in Ministral allowed for the improvement of the results of combined T9+T18 from 10/40 (25%) to 25/40 (62.5%) without any changes in the model parameters used; later attempts of the GPT using different approaches also yielded a much higher percentage of 39/40 (97.5). Being aware that the later records were not independent and controlled tests of model size also allow us to draw the conclusion of the study itself, which states that although scale contributes significantly to the development of the most complicated problems, search technique and verification practice assist in minimizing a gap by eliminating.

title: Berna R8: Bounded Forgetting in Cell-Based Language Models (Proof of Concept)
abstract: Berna R8 is a proof-of-concept follow-up to Berna R7 v3. It fixes five architectural issues identified in R7 v3 (per-cell K5 freshness, per-cell K6 encompassment, per-cell K2 breadth, Plexus threshold, and full DNA persistence) and implements Bounded Forgetting — the central claim of the parent theory R5 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23015308). The H2 experiment demonstrates for the first time that fine-tuning Berna on a new language (German, 2000 steps) improves the target language (DE loss: 4.7406 → 4.0797) without degrading the original language (ENG loss: 4.0781 → 4.0703). The forgetting metric F_eng = max(0, ENG_after - ENG_before) = 0.000000, satisfying the R5 bounded-forgetting criterion (F_j ≤ 1e-6). The R8 model weights and code are available at https://huggingface.co/BernaLabs/berna-r8.

title: Educational innovation: intelligent tutoring systems for learning in the university environment
abstract: Higher education is undergoing constant transformation driven by information and communication technologies, with platforms such as Moodle and mobile devices fostering collaborative activities in the classroom. In this context, intelligent tutoring systems are emerging as innovative tools to strengthen educational processes worldwide. The aim of this research is to understand lecturers’ perceptions of the integration of intelligent tutoring systems in the context of teaching computer engineering at the Ezequiel Zamora National Experimental University of the Western Plains. To this end, a qualitative methodology was employed under the interpretative paradigm, utilising a phenomenological-hermeneutic field design of an emergent and negotiated nature, achieving an integrative level of complexity. The key informants were five lecturers from the university’s Computer Engineering sub-programme. The findings show that lecturers perceive ITS as pedagogical mediators; they significantly increase learning outcomes, maintain student motivation, and transform teaching into a collaborative process between lecturer and student. It is concluded that these tools reduce drop-out rates and improve academic performance, substantially benefiting the educational process.

title: Artificial intelligence at the surgeon–pathologist interface: revolutionizing diagnosis, prognostication, and precision surgery
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applications in surgical pathology encompass tumour detection, histological classification, grading, biomarker assessment, lymph node evaluation, margin analysis, and outcome prediction. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high diagnostic performance across multiple malignancies including breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Emerging computational pathology platforms can predict molecular alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, facilitating personalized treatment strategies while reducing dependence on expensive ancillary testing. AI-assisted pathology has also improved workflow efficiency, reduced interobserver variability, and enhanced diagnostic reproducibility. Importantly, AI-derived pathological insights are increasingly influencing surgical decision-making through improved risk stratification, optimized extent of resection, tailored lymphadenectomy, and prediction of treatment response.

title: Classical-Tutor: A Dual-Role RAG Architecture for Classical Document Resources in Digital Libraries
abstract: Classical documents in digital libraries—such as Classical Chinese texts—are not only valuable cultural heritage but also core educational resources at the foundational education level. However, existing digital library systems predominantly focus on full-text retrieval and basic machine translation, making it difficult to support learners' deep cognitive construction. Meanwhile, the direct integration of large language models (LLMs) tends to trap learners in an answer-seeking mode, thereby diminishing the inquiry-based thinking essential to the humanities. This paper proposes and implements Classical-Tutor, an intelligent tutoring system for Classical Chinese digital resources. The system deeply integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a curriculum knowledge graph and introduces a graph-based dual-role dynamic scheduling engine (Dual-Role State Machine). Through a multi-trigger mechanism, the system adaptively switches between knowledge lecturing and heuristic guiding. In an LLM-simulated pilot evaluation the system sustains longer instructional interaction than a baseline RAG system, adapts retrieval granularity to learner profiles, and avoids the deadlocks of static Socratic prompting; the results characterize orchestration behavior rather than learning gains. The study offers an architectural reference for the intelligent utilization of humanities special collections in digital libraries.

title: Learning Operators for Symmetry Discovery: From Lie Groups to Local Symmetry Geometry
abstract: Continuous symmetry discovery is typically formulated as a separate estimation problem for each function or dataset. We instead investigate whether the map from a function to its symmetry structure can be learned across a family of functions from finite observations. Using the infinitesimal differential characterization of continuous symmetries, we formulate this map as an inverse symmetry operator, analogous to an inverse PDE problem. For global Lie-group symmetries, we establish a representation-theoretic population characterization: the symmetry Lie algebra is the nullspace of a positive-semidefinite operator constructed from representation coefficients and the infinitesimal group action. We also show that the inverse symmetry operator is equivariant under coordinate changes through the adjoint action. This characterization separates the geometric symmetry map from finite-sample estimation, motivating a hybrid approach that amortizes statistically difficult components while retaining analytic structure. On SO(5) benchmarks, amortized equivariant estimation of harmonic coefficients improves symmetry recovery from sparse observations, whereas ordinary least squares suffices for SL(2,R). We extend this viewpoint to local symmetries, where symmetry directions form smoothly varying tangent distributions rather than a fixed Lie algebra. Under the Lie-bracket consistency condition, Frobenius' theorem guarantees local integral submanifolds along which observables remain unchanged. We recover this geometry using a hybrid estimator that learns observation weights while preserving analytic differential and geometric recovery. Across global, non-compact, local, and physically motivated synthetic benchmarks, our results support learning the statistically difficult finite-sample components while preserving the known geometric structure of symmetry recovery.

title: SkillFusion: Towards Reliable Multi-Skill Composition for LLM Agents
abstract: Independently authored skills can impose incompatible requirements, competing preferences, and redundant instructions when jointly loaded by an LLM agent. We propose SkillFusion, an offline compiler that reconciles these interactions into a reusable merged skill. Its central idea is to make composition decisions explicit through typed, scoped constraints linked to their source directives. A type-scope gate selects candidate interactions, while selective fallback revisits pairs potentially missed by structural pruning. A classifier identifies interaction types, and an adversarial verifier re-examines uncertain judgments. The resolver applies conditional routing or explicit priorities to hard conflicts, verified abstraction to soft conflicts, and deduplication to redundant instructions. Source-linked checks guide synthesis and compression, and metadata synthesis supports discovery of the merged skill. The resulting artifact retains associated scripts and resources and can be reused across tasks and executor models. SkillFusion achieves the highest mean Success among evaluated non-oracle methods on all three agent benchmarks and on both transfer benchmarks across three executor models. At the largest tested instruction configurations, it achieves over 2.5 times the Success of unresolved multi-skill loading, highlighting the growing value of reconciliation as composition becomes more demanding. The code will be open-sourced after the review process concludes.

title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.

title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners
abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision
abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.

title: Handoff Curves: Initial Selection, Later Handoff, and Supervision Targets in Multi-turn LLM Routing
abstract: We study how initial model selection, later handoff, and training targets affect success and cost in LLM tasks that span multiple turns. We compare several router architectures using handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step changes. Our dataset contains 34,204 complete executions of three Qwen models across BFCL, MultiWOZ, and $τ$-retail, providing offline supervision for routing decisions. In our primary comparison, with Qwen3.5 35B-A3B as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not establish an improvement in utility over initial selection on BFCL or MultiWOZ, and increases cost on BFCL across a range of cost weights. Changing the supervision targets improves router performance on both our dataset and TwinRouterBench. On our dataset, replacing noisy training success curves with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at the same cost across the reported operating points. On TwinRouterBench, we construct targets that describe the model capability needed for the remaining work and difficult steps ahead. Compared with training on the benchmark's per-step labels, these targets raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 percentage points on the full static bank. A live deployment of the router trained with these targets resolves 79 of 100 instances at a router cost of 0.59 US dollars per instance.

title: Latent-Space Importance Weighting under Covariate Shift
abstract: In this work, we propose a transfer learning algorithm for covariate shift, integrating sample reweighting with representation learning. A key feature of our approach is the use of a lower-dimensional latent space for modeling, in contrast to conventional methods that operate directly in the high-dimensional ambient space. Our method estimates the density ratio of learned latent features for downstream weighted prediction. We establish explicit target-domain excess-risk rates with independent data folds for strictly sufficient learned representations with regular learned-space prediction scores and density ratios. We give dimension comparisons under stated smoothness conditions and a variance comparison for true weights and a fixed predictor. General finite-sample inequalities retain representation-quality errors. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate gains from combining learned representations and latent weighting, and reveal sensitivity to initialization and domain choice.

title: CIViC: Evidence Gates for Audio-Conditioned Visual Prediction on Proxy Tasks
abstract: Removing audio can shift a visual predictor's output without showing whether the task uses the intended audio information. We introduce Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks (CIViC), a four-gate protocol that links an interpretation to an intervention, held-out task comparison, or endpoint control. We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.

title: An Explainable System for Offensive Content Detection in Nastaliq Urdu: Corpus Curation, Transformer Benchmarking, and Word-Level Attribution
abstract: Automated moderation systems are deployed at scale, yet they remain opaque to the users and moderators affected by their decisions, and their coverage is almost entirely confined to English. For Urdu written in the Nastaliq script, no such system exists, and the annotated resources it would be built on are drawn largely from Twitter/X, where character limits constrain how users write. Interpretability has received little attention, leaving it unclear what such models actually learn. This study addresses these gaps in three steps. First, we curate and publicly release a corpus of 7604 Nastaliq Urdu Facebook comments, extending an earlier corpus by correcting text-level inconsistencies and re-examining the original labels. Second, we fine-tune four Urdu-capable transformers under a common grid-search protocol and compare them against twelve feature-classifier baselines on identical data partitions. The best configuration, Multilingual Representations for Indian Languages (MuRIL), reaches 87.05% accuracy and 87.06% macro F1, improving on the strongest baseline by 5.52 percentage points, a margin that exceeds the 95% confidence interval on test accuracy; the two leading transformers differ by less than the test set can resolve, and performance is stable across five optimizers. Third, we compute word-level SHAP attributions adapted to right-to-left rendering. Attribution mass concentrates on high-frequency slurs but extends to syntactically neutral function words and to political vocabulary characteristic of the source pages, indicating that aggregate performance may rest partly on lexical and topical regularities rather than a generalizable representation of offensiveness.

title: EvolvAttack: Backdooring self Evolving VLM Agents
abstract: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.

title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.

title: An Interpretable Linguistically-Grounded Analysis of Scene Saliency in Movie Screenplays
abstract: We investigate the factors affecting salience in movie screenplay by posing two research questions: 1. {\em Does Uniform Information Density (UID) predict salient scenes?} 2. {\em What other linguistic properties distinguish salient scenes from non-salient background?} We answer both questions through a controlled corpus study on the MENSA corpus, paired with a Linguistically-Grounded Salience Model (LGSM), a dual-stream classifier that fuses a frozen BERT encoder with explicit linguistic features through adaptive gating. The UID picture is layered in long-form discourse. Per-scene UID summaries carry no independent signal once length is controlled, but at the token level salient scenes match non-salient material in the bulk while specifically suppressing the rarest, hardest-to-predict tokens in the upper tail. UID therefore lives at the within-scene token level rather than as a per-scene aggregate. Salient scenes also show a moderate and sustained cast of central characters (following an inverted-U pattern), strong third-person usage, syntactically simpler language, and more abstract vocabulary about motivation and conflict. LGSM exploits this signature and improves recall on salient scenes over a strong semantic baseline while yielding better downstream summaries.

title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.

title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.

title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.

title: RetryBench: Separating Retry Permission from Recovery Outcomes in GPT Tool Use
abstract: False retry permission (FRP) occurs when an agent retries a timed-out tool call without support from the visible contract. RetryBench separates this error from realized recovery. Successful protected recovery does not imply reliable rejection of unsupported retries. In a 720-response key control, valid keys usually enabled safe progress, but offered changed keys elicited unsupported retries in Sol (1/80), Terra (55/80), and Luna (60/80). A later 240-response control removed the candidate and required models to supply a key. Luna still made 8/80 unsupported dispatches; Sol and Terra made none in 80 responses each. Accepting a displayed bad key therefore cannot explain all observed errors, although changed output requirements and conditions preclude a pure display-effect comparison. Removing the weak-contract label increased retries in Sol and Terra's coded-action conditions in a six-endpoint study. A separate 1,536-response canonical-action block also found a positive Terra contrast (115/128 versus 124/128 retries), concentrated in two task/order conditions; the other five contrasts remained unresolved after multiplicity correction. An explicit-contract cue control elicited deferral in all 762 returned responses, leaving recovery unresolved. These results support reporting permission and recovery together across declared interface variants. The evidence covers four purposive tasks, fixed GPT endpoints, and one recovery decision; it identifies neither internal mechanisms nor episode-level safety.

title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.

title: Who Sets the Pace of Judge Hacking? Judge Capability versus the Policy-Judge Gap
abstract: Under GRPO against a frozen, reference-free LLM judge, RL exploits the judge's false positives. Does the policy-judge capability gap or the judge itself set how fast and how far? We train 0.5B and 1.5B Qwen2.5 policies on GSM8K against four judges at least as large, and the 1.5B policy also against one smaller judge. In a post-hoc analysis, judge acceptance rose, but no cell of 12 gained more than 0.04 in seed-mean held-out greedy accuracy. A gold-reward control with the same recipe raised the 1.5B policy's accuracy by +0.054 (for the 0.5B policy, gold reward gave no detectable gain either). The depth of judge hacking tracks the judge: the plateau correlates with judge AUC (Spearman -0.69 over 12 cells), and within a family the larger judge is fooled less deeply. For the pace, two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account: the cell with the larger gap was fooled 3.5x sooner at the pre-specified threshold. With 12 cells, however, we cannot formally separate judge AUC from the gap for either endpoint. A blind test of step-0 predictors on three held-out judges was inconclusive. At 7-8B, judges from three families plateaued between 0.37 and 0.85.

title: RSIPO: Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Skill-Policy Co-Evolution
abstract: Recent focus in agentic reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks. One promising direction combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), integrating trajectory-level advantages with dense token-level supervision. This line of work often conditions a teacher model on privileged context, such as agentic skills, to score tokens generated by the student policy. Despite their progress, they largely overlook the on-policy evolution of agentic skills and the reliability of teacher supervision. Towards this end, we introduce Recursive Self-Improving Policy Optimization (RSIPO), a self-evolving agentic RL framework that enables agentic skills and the policy model to co-evolve throughout the training process. Specifically, RSIPO enables the policy itself to extract skills from completed trajectories and explicitly optimizes its skill-generation capability through trajectory replay. It further employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to dynamically calibrate the student's trust in teacher scores, accounting for the fact that skill-enhanced teacher guidance can sometimes be less reliable. Experiments with Qwen-family models on embodied interaction and search-based agentic tasks demonstrate that RSIPO outperforms all the compared baseline approaches. With Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, RSIPO achieves an average success rate of 98.6\% on ALFWorld, yielding absolute improvements of 2.5\% and 17.4\% over the second-best baseline and standard GRPO, respectively.

title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.

title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
abstract: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.

title: What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify? From Activations to Interventions
abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are typically discovered from how their activations co-vary with behaviour, yet they are often used through interventions such as steering or ablation. We take intervention attribution, the first-order effect of a specified intervention on the model output, as our estimand. For a broad class of response functions, we show that observational feature-discovery evidence generally does not identify this attribution, and derive an exact gradient-based decomposition of the gap between linear-probe predictions and intervention attribution. Across four model-SAE pairs, median probe-to-attribution magnitude ratios range from tens to hundreds, while attributions closely track small-step steering. For single-latent ablations with nonzero effects, gradient predictions match the realized sign in 91-97% of cases, compared with 17-35% for probe-implied changes. Attribution-selected sets also produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than sets selected by correlation, rank tests or probe coefficients. Together, these results establish intervention attribution as a principled, gradient-estimable target for selecting SAE features for intervention.

title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized: Formation, Maintenance, and Latent Susceptibility
abstract: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization's formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility.
